question: What is the ﬁrst-line oral antibiotic in the treatment of ocular Lyme disease (LD)?
explanation: Ocular LD is typically treated in the same manner as central nervous system (CNS) LD. The antibiotics doxycycline, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone (and other penicillin family members) are most eﬀective in treating ocular LD. Chloramphenicol, a broad-spectrum antibiotic, is typically administered intravenously and orally but is also available as an ophthalmic suspension outside the US. Chloramphenicol has been used to treat intraocular rickettsial infections (gram-negative arthropod-borne bacteria), but not the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, the etiologic agent causing LD. Ciproﬂoxacin, a ﬂuoroquinolone, has good coverage against gram- negative bacteria, but it is not as eﬀective in treating spirochetal infections as doxycycline and the penicillin-family antibiotics.

question: What type of macrophage expresses major histocompatibility (MHC) class II antigen, can function as an antigen- presenting cell to T lymphocytes, and can exit tissue sites by aﬀerent lymphatic vessels to reenter lymph nodes?
explanation: Resting macrophages are the classic scavenging cells, capable of phagocytosis and uptake of dead cell membranes, chemically modiﬁed extracellular protein (ie, acetylated or oxidized lipoproteins), sugar ligands, naked nucleic acids, and bacterial pathogens. Resting monocytes express at least 3 types of scavenging receptors but synthesize very low levels of proinﬂammatory cytokines. Scavenging can occur in the absence of inﬂammation.

question: What immunoglobulin has the highest concentration in the blood serum?
explanation: The correct answer is IgG. There are 5 major classes of immunoglobulins: IgA, IgG, IgM, IgE, and IgD. The most common immunoglobulin found in blood serum is IgG, followed by IgA, IgM, and then IgD and IgE. An immunoglobulin is composed of 2 domains: the Fab (fragment, antigen-binding) and the Fc (fragment crystallizable). The Fab portion is the antigen recognition-combining domain, also called the hypervariable region. The Fc region is the attachment site for eﬀector cells, activating various pathways such as complement activation. IgG is a monomer, and found mostly in the intravascular serum. IgG is signiﬁcant in that it can cross the placenta. IgG contributes to more than 50% of the serum immunoglobulins. Their Fc region binds to a variety of cells, including monocytes and killer lymphocytes. These participate in both antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and cytolysis. IgA is found predominately in mucosa secretions. It is a monomer in serum, but it is a dimer in secretions. Its main function is mucosal immunity and neutralization. IgM is found mostly on B lymphocytes or in the intravascular space. Its structure is a pentamer or hexameter, and it is a strong activator of the complement system. It is also important to know that IgM is the primary immune response to new antigens (and will be elevated immediately after infection), whereas IgG is a mature immune response to antigens previously processed. IgE is a monomer that is found mostly in skin or mucosa. Its Fc domain binds mast cells, causing degranulation of the mast cell and recruitment of eosinophils.

question: By what mechanism is mycophenolate mofetil thought to ameliorate autoimmune uveitis?

options.A: crosslinking DNA in rapidly dividing cells
options.D: inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and DNA synthesis

explanation: Mycophenolate mofetil inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, which prevents the synthesis of the purine nucleotide guanosine. This prevents B and T lymphocyte synthesis, and leads to aberrant base pairing, ring cleavage, and depurination, which leads to cell death. Inhibition of bacterial ribosomes characterizes the mechanism of action of some antibiotics (for example streptomycin, erythromycin, and chloramphenicol). Therapies that reliably induce immunologic tolerance in autoinﬂammatory conditions are being developed, but they have yet to show eﬃcacy in uveitis.

A 29-year-old White man presents with gradually worsening nyctalopia and decreasing vision over several years. His visual acuity is 20/30; there are rare anterior chamber cells, trace vitreous cells, and macular edema; and the retinal periphery has bone spicule pigmentation in both eyes. There is no history of trauma. He reports multiple sexual partners. There is no history of any eye disease in the family. What test would most likely reveal a speciﬁc etiology for his ﬁndings?
explanation: Although this could be birdshot chorioretinopathy, an HLA-A29 test will be positive in 7% or more of whites; therefore, this test does not by itself make the diagnosis. In addition, such advanced birdshot chorioretinopathy would be rare in this age group. Retinitis pigmentosa should also be in the diﬀerential, but neither ERG nor visual ﬁeld is speciﬁc for the diagnosis and can be abnormal in many processes, including birdshot chorioretinopathy and syphilis, where the retina is involved. Although it is important to perform these tests, they will not enable a speciﬁc diagnosis to be made. A syphilitic etiology, which can masquerade as noninfectious uveitis, should also be on the diﬀerential list. A speciﬁc treponemal serologic test should be checked to rule out this infectious process. A positive speciﬁc treponemal serologic test result without a history of being treated for syphilis should warrant treatment of this condition.

question: What topical corticosteroid medication is most likely to cause a corticosteroid-response elevation in IOP?
explanation: Of the choices listed, prednisolone acetate 1% demonstrates the greatest eﬀect of decreasing intraocular inﬂammation, and the greatest eﬀect of increasing IOP. Rimexolone has a slightly less potent eﬀect. Fluorometholone is a very potent corticosteroid, but penetrates poorly into the eye and therefore is less likely to result in an increase in IOP. Loteprednol is also less likely to raise IOP. Diﬂuprednate, a newer corticosteroid, may have a similar rate of elevation of IOP. Clinical studies suggest diﬂuprednate has a similar adverse eﬀect proﬁle to prednisolone, but is associated with potentially higher rises in IOP.

explanation: The patient in this clinical scenario has granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). Of GPA patients treated with cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids, 93% successfully achieve remission. Oocyte harvest and banking is prudent in a patient about to start cyclophosphamide who plans future pregnancies. Cyclophosphamide interferes with oogenesis and spermatogenesis. It may cause sterility in both sexes, and in some patients this may be irreversible. Other well- established adverse eﬀects include teratogenicity, hemorrhagic cystitis, and development of secondary malignancies. Variants in the gene encoding thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) alter its activity and may contribute to increased risk of hematologic events or leukopenia in treatment with thiopurines (eg, azathioprine), not cyclophosphamide. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan/bone densitometry detects osteopenia/osteoporosis. It is useful in long-term corticosteroid administration, but osteopenia is not a signiﬁcant risk of cyclophosphamide use. Transesophageal echocardiogram detects cardiac and valvular structural abnormalities. Cardiac valve disease is not a signiﬁcant risk of cyclophosphamide use, although acute cardiotoxicity has been reported in the setting of antineoplastic multi-drug therapy and transplant procedures involving this drug.

question: By what mode is the chikungunya virus typically transmitted to humans?
explanation: Chikungunya fever, a potentially fatal illness, is caused by single- stranded RNA virus of the genus Alphavirus, in the family Togaviridae. It is transmitted via infected mosquitoes including Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Toxoplasma gondii can be transmitted via ingestion of contaminated water, fruit, or vegetables with oocysts. HIV/AIDS, hepatitis B virus, and hepatitis C virus are among the diseases transmitted by contact with blood or bodily ﬂuids. Common pathogens transmitted via drinking water are norovirus, Giardia, Legionella, Salmonella, and Escherichia coli.

question: A patient with retinal vasculitis also has necrotizing pulmonary granulomas and nephritis. What serum antibody is most likely to be associated with this entity?

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is the most likely condition that would ﬁt this description; therefore, the correct serum antibody is ANCA. Approximately 10% of patients with GPA can manifest retinal vascular involvement. Systemic lupus erythematosus (as suggested by ANA) does not result in pulmonary granulomas, although it can produce a retinal vasculitis and nephritis.

question: What is the pathogen associated with the development of Kaposi sarcoma?
explanation: The pathogen involved with the development of Kaposi sarcoma is human herpesvirus (HHV)-8. HHV-4 is also known as Epstein-Barr virus and is associated with the development of primary central nervous system lymphomas and primary vitreoretinal lymphomas in HIV- infected individuals. question: What should be the initial treatment of neovascularization of the disc in a patient with sarcoid-related panuveitis?

explanation: Retinal neovascularization in uveitis results from chronic inﬂammation or capillary nonperfusion. Sarcoid panuveitis may be complicated with neovascularization of the disc and resolves completely with immunomodulatory and corticosteroid therapy alone. Uveitides with retinal vasculitis may cause retinal neovascularization due to ischemia and thus may necessitate retinal laser photocoagulation or intravitreal anti-VEGF injection. Treatment of subfoveal choroidal neovascularization (CNV) is accomplished with VEGF inhibitors; photodynamic therapy with verteporﬁn may be an adjunctive treatment. In all cases, however, control of inﬂammation is paramount; this also reduces the risk of recurrence of CNV.

question: The major criteria of diagnosing Behçet disease (BD) include oral ulceration and what other ﬁnding?
explanation: The diagnosis of BD is based entirely on clinical ﬁndings. The diagnostic criteria, according to the International Study Group for Behçet's disease, include recurrent oral and genital ulcers, ocular inﬂammation, skin lesions, and a positive cutaneous pathergy test. Although arthritis, as well as cardiac, gastrointestinal, pulmonary, and central nervous system (CNS) involvement, have been reported in patients with Behçet disease, these are not major criteria for diagnosis.

question: Based on epidemiologic data, what is the most common type of uveitis patient an ophthalmologist is likely to encounter?

options.A: a 26-year-old white man with a negative review of systems who presents with sudden-onset unilateral pain, redness, decreased vision, and photophobia
options.B: a 32-year-old white woman with multiple sclerosis (MS) who presents with subacute onset of ﬂoaters in both eyes
options.C: a 28-year-old Hispanic man with 3 cats at home who presents with sudden onset of ﬂoaters and worsening vision in his left eye
options.D: a 38-year-old woman of Native American descent who presents with sudden-onset ﬂoaters and decreased vision and, on examination, found to have bilateral exudative retinal detachments

explanation: Epidemiologically, the most common form of uveitis is anterior uveitis, followed by panuveitis, posterior uveitis, and lastly, intermediate uveitis. The patient with a negative review of systems who presents with sudden-onset unilateral pain, redness, decreased vision, and photophobia likely has HLA-B27-associated acute anterior uveitis. The patient with MS has intermediate uveitis secondary to her MS. The patient who has cats likely has posterior uveitis secondary to toxoplasmosis. The patient with bilateral exudative retinal detachments likely has panuveitis secondary to Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome. (Aside: while HLA-B27 acute anterior uveitis is classically associated with one of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies [ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, enterohepatic arthritis, psoriatic arthritis] it is more common for a B27 (+) patient to present with acute anterior uveitis in the absence of any systemic manifestations, as opposed to ﬁrst being diagnosed with one of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies and then presenting with acute anterior uveitis).

question: The treatment of cystoid macular edema associated with active uveitis should begin with what therapy?

options.C: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) antibody injection

explanation: Cystoid macular edema (CME) is a common cause of vision loss in eyes with uveitis. Treatment of CME must ﬁrst be directed toward control of intraocular inﬂammation, for which topical steroid remains ﬁrst-line therapy. If CME persists despite control of inﬂammation, periocular injection of corticosteroid may be used. Typically, 20-40 mg of triamcinolone is injected into the sub-Tenon space. Anti-VEGF therapies can also reduce inﬂammatory CME, but the action is short lived and repeat injections are required. Topical NSAIDs can be beneﬁcial in treating pseudophakic CME, but their eﬀectiveness in treating uveitic CME is not established. Oral acetazolamide has been shown to reduce uveitic CME in patients whose uveitis is well controlled.

question: What uveitis therapy has the highest risk of causing secondary glaucoma severe enough to require pressure- lowering surgery?
explanation: Corticosteroids via any route carry the risk of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in predisposed patients. Topical corticosteroids carry the lowest risk. Periocular and intravitreal corticosteroid injections more commonly lead to elevated IOP that requires ﬁltering surgery in 1% to 2% of patients. The intravitreal ﬂuocinolone implant leads to elevated IOP that requires glaucoma therapy in about 75% of patients and glaucoma surgery in about 37% of patients. Antimetabolites such as methotrexate have not been reported to directly lead to elevated IOP.

A 3-month-old child with seizures who was born in an area noted to have mouse droppings is referred by the pediatric department for ophthalmologic examination. Abnormalities were noted on computed tomography (CT) scan and clinical examination. What antibody titer is most likely to be elevated in both mother and patient?
explanation: Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is a fetal teratogen, passed vertically from mother to fetus during pregnancy. Rodents are the natural host and reservoir, and infection to the mother usually occurs after eating food contaminated with infected rodent excrement or by the bite of an infected rodent. The earlier in pregnancy a mother is infected, the more severe the sequelae in the developing fetus. Manifestations in a child born to a mother infected with LCMV during pregnancy include macrocephaly, hydrocephalus, periventricular calciﬁcations with seizures, chorioretinal scars (very similar to toxoplasmosis scars), optic atrophy, nystagmus, and strabismus. Toxoplasma gondii can present very similarly when transmitted to a fetus; however, the intracranial calciﬁcations in congenital toxoplasmosis infection tend to be diﬀuse (as opposed to periventricular), and the natural hosts and reservoirs of Toxoplasma gondii are cats. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection in a fetus can cause intracranial calciﬁcations and hydrocephalus, but does not produce chorioretinal scarring. Syphilis infection in a fetus does not typically produce intracranial calciﬁcations or hydrocephalus, and again chorioretinal scarring is absent (syphilis infection can produce a diﬀuse, "salt-and-pepper" pigmentary retinopathy).

question: When stellate keratic precipitates are present in herpes simplex type 1 intraocular infections, how are they typically distributed on the corneal endothelium?

options.B: in the inferior third of the cornea (Arlt triangle)
options.D: keratic precipitates are not found in herpes simplex type 1 intraocular infections

explanation: Stellate keratic precipitates (KPs) are very suggestive of a viral intraocular infection and are frequently seen. However, in herpetic intraocular infections, particularly with herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2 as well as varicella-zoster virus, there may be nongranulomatous or granulomatous KPs as well. In this question, stellate KPs are identiﬁed and, when present, often are found diﬀusely. The KPs localizing only to the inferior third of the cornea (Arlt triangle) are classically found in noninfectious etiologies of intraocular inﬂammation and may be either granulomatous or nongranulomatous. Coin-shaped lesions are found in cytomegalovirus anterior uveitis.

explanation: Treatment of CMV retinitis involves 3 steps: immune reconstitution with HAART and concomitant treatment of the virus (intravenous ganciclovir or foscarnet, oral valganciclovir, or intravitreal ganciclovir or foscarnet [see Table 11-3]); maintenance of antiviral therapy for 3-6 months to allow for adequate immune reconstitution (despite early recovery of CD4+ cell counts); continued HAART therapy without antivirals, with dilated fundus examinations every 3 months (because immune reconstitution uveitis [IRU] can occur in patients on HAART with a history of prior CMV retinitis, even if the retinitis is currently inactive and CD4+ counts are >50 cells/µL; IRU tends to occur more frequently in eyes with more than 25% of the retinal surface involved in prior CMV infections). In the case described, at 10 months out from initial infection, on HAART, and with CD4+ counts of 200 cells/µL, this patient is immune reconstituted from a CMV risk standpoint and can safely be observed oﬀ antiviral treatment with dilated fundus examinations every 3 months. (Note that the ganciclovir implant lasts for approximately 8 months, which is ample time to allow for immune reconstitution on HAART, as oral valganciclovir therapy in this setting is typically discontinued 6 months after the initiation of HAART). There is no need to replace or remove the ganciclovir implant in the absence of new signs of CMV infection, which is unlikely at CD4+ counts >50 cells/µL (although, as stated earlier, IRU can still occur while patients are on HAART, and as such these patients should be monitored every 3 months).

question: A 48-year-old patient has nyctalopia and decreased vision. Given the color photo and angiographic image shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Patients with birdshot retinochoroidopathy present with blurred vision, ﬂoaters, and nyctalopia. Funduscopy reveals characteristic multifocal, hypopigmented, ovoid, cream-colored lesions at the level of the choroid and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in postequatorial, mostly nasal fundus in a radial pattern, as shown in the images (Fig. 1). Cystoid macular edema (CME), as shown in the fundus ﬂuorescein angiogram (FA) below, is a common reason for decreased vision in these patients and a sign of disease activity. Punctate inner choroiditis (PIC) commonly presents in otherwise healthy myopic white women at a younger median age (29-45 years). Lesions of PIC rarely extend to the midperiphery, and CME is uncommon. Choroidal neovascularization is a common vision- threatening complication. Lesions in MEWDS are distributed perifoveally and are discrete, white- orange spots (as shown in Fig. 2). question: What agent used in the therapy of uveitis may induce antichimeric antibodies?
explanation: Inﬂiximab is a mouse/human-chimeric, immunoglobulin G1 kappa (IgG1k) monoclonal antibody directed against tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-a. As many as 75% of patients receiving more than 3 infusions developed antinuclear antibodies, thus causing drug-induced lupus syndrome and the formation of human antichimeric antibodies, which can lead to reduced eﬃcacy of inﬂiximab. Abatacept is a T-cell costimulation inhibitor given as an intravenous infusion. Interferon alfa-2a/2b (IFN- a2a/b), administered subcutaneously, has been reported to be beneﬁcial in some patients with uveitis. IFN- a2a has antiviral, immunomodulatory, and antiangiogenic eﬀects. Tacrolimus, a product of Streptomyces tsukubaensis, is a calcineurin inhibitor that eliminates T-cell receptor signal transduction and downregulates interleukin-2 gene transcription and receptor expression of CD4 T lymphocytes. Abatacept, IFN- a2a/b, and tacrolimus are not associated with formation of antibodies. +.

explanation: Melanomas can be associated with an impressive inﬂammatory response, and ciliary body melanomas can break through to the anterior segment. The diﬀerential diagnosis includes infections, chronic retinal detachment, and metastatic tumors. question: What type of lymphocytes participate in the innate immune response?

options.C: natural killer cells and intraepithelial lymphocytes

explanation: Lymphocytes include B cells, T cells, and non-B, non-T lymphocytes. Two types of lymphocytes participate in the innate immune response: 1) gamma-delta (γδ) T cells or sentinel T cells, also known as intraepithelial lymphocytes, and 2) natural killer cells. These serve as a bridge between innate and adaptive responses. Eosinophils are important in allergic immune reactions and parasitic infections. Basophils are the blood-borne equivalent of tissue-bound mast cells, which act as major eﬀector cells in IgE-mediated inﬂammatory reactions. Langerhans cells are myeloid cells with dendritic cell function.

question: Among the white dot syndromes, for what disorder are the lesions on ﬂuorescein angiography (FA) least apparent?

explanation: FA in birdshot uveitis reveals inconsistent ﬁndings depending on the age of the lesions and the phase of the study. Early birdshot uveitis lesions can show initial hypoﬂuorescence with subtle late staining. In general, however, FA does not typically highlight the lesions themselves, but rather is useful in identifying more subtle types of active inﬂammation such as retinal vasculitis, cystoid macular edema, and optic nerve head leakage. In contrast, in patients with acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE), FA shows characteristic early blockage with late staining of the lesions, and in patients with punctate inner choroiditis (PIC), it reveals early hyperﬂuorescence with late staining of BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A pseudophakic 52-year-old man complains of ﬂoaters and is found to have anterior chamber ﬂare and cells in the anterior vitreous. He has a laser demarcation around an inferior retinal detachment. What is the most likely cause of his cell and ﬂare?
explanation: Chronic peripheral rhegmatogenous retinal detachment can be associated with anterior segment cell and ﬂare, along with vitreous cells. Patients often have good vision that can sometimes deteriorate because of cystoid macular edema (CME). Careful dilated fundus examination with scleral depression is of paramount importance in establishing the diagnosis. Findings may include peripheral pigment demarcation lines, subretinal ﬂuid, retinal breaks, subretinal ﬁbrosis, and peripheral retinal cysts. Photoreceptor outer segments liberated from the subretinal space may be present in the anterior chamber, simulating inﬂammatory cells. In such situations, intraocular pressure (IOP) may be elevated, as these photoreceptor outer segments are phagocytosed by the endothelial cells in the trabecular meshwork, resulting in secondary open-angle glaucoma. This condition is called Schwartz syndrome; however, the condition is rare and speciﬁc to very anteriorized tears in the retina, involving the vitreous base, that give shed photoreceptor outer segments access to the anterior chamber (otherwise, with more posterior tears, photoreceptor outer segments would be trapped in the posterior segment by an intact hyaloid face). cidofovir.

explanation: Foscarnet and ganciclovir are medications appropriate as intravitreal preparations for the treatment of CMV retinitis. Of the choices listed here, foscarnet is the best. Valganciclovir is the L-valyl ester prodrug of ganciclovir. The valine increases both the absorption of the drug in the intestines and the bioavailability of the drug once it is absorbed. Cidofovir was previously used as intravitreal therapy for the treatment of CMV, especially in the pre-highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) era, but this medication is associated with hypotonous uveitis, which can lead to blindness. Acyclovir is not appropriate for CMV, because acyclovir needs to be phosphorylated by a viral thymidine kinase (TK) and CMV lacks TK.

question: What stage of Vogt-Koyanagi- Harada syndrome is most likely to be associated with exudative retinal detachments?
explanation: The acute uveitic stage is typically associated with exudative retinal detachments. By deﬁnition, the prodromal stage is characterized by systemic symptoms such as a ﬂulike syndrome and headaches prior to the development of clinically apparent ophthalmic disease. The convalescent stage occurs weeks to months after the exudative retinal detachments have resolved; patients can develop gradual depigmentation in the fundus and ﬁndings such as vitiligo, alopecia, and poliosis. The chronic recurrent stage is associated with repeated bouts of anterior uveitis that can lead to signiﬁcant structural damage, but it is not commonly associated with recurrence of the exudative retinal detachments.

question: A patient with necrotizing scleritis is found to have antibodies directed against proteinase 3. What disease is most likely to be associated with this ﬁnding?
explanation: Testing for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) involves 2 techniques: (1) immunoﬂuorescent testing, which evaluates for the presence of cytoplasmic or perinuclear immunoﬂuorescence patterns (c-ANCA and p-ANCA, respectively), and (2) testing for the speciﬁc antibodies that cause each immunoﬂuorescent pattern. Antibodies to proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA) are associated with c-ANCA, and antibodies to myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA) are associated with p-ANCA. Tests for PR3-ANCA and c-ANCA are sensitive and speciﬁc for granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Positivity for MPO-ANCA and p- ANCA is more commonly associated with microscopic polyangiitis. Approximately 50% of patients with Churg-Strauss syndrome test positive for ANCA; they are typically, but not uniformly, MPO-ANCA positive. In a patient with antibodies to proteinase 3, the most likely associated disease will be granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

question: What important condition may mimic human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) uveitis?

options.D: idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis (IRVAN)

explanation: Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1), a retrovirus of the Oncovirinae subfamily, is endemic in Japan, the Caribbean islands, and parts of Central and South America. The major target cell of HTLV-1 is the CD4+ T cell. HTLV-1 infection is the established cause of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL), HTLV-1–associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paralysis (HAM/TSP), and HTLV-1 uveitis (HU), deﬁned as uveitis of undetermined origin in an HTLV-1 carrier. HU is responsive to corticosteroid therapy. For cases that progress despite adequate therapy, the clinician must consider a masquerade syndrome, as both retinal inﬁltration caused by ATL and retinal degeneration associated with HAM/TSP have been shown to mimic HU.

question: What laboratory parameter requires regular monitoring with use of systemic cyclosporine?
explanation: Nephrotoxicity and hypertension are the major systemic side eﬀects of cyclosporine. Serum creatinine should be monitored regularly with patients taking cyclosporine, and dosage adjustments are needed if it rises 30% or more above baseline. Sustained elevation may require discontinuation of this medication. Systemic hypertension is another major side eﬀect of cyclosporine, and the blood pressure of patients taking cyclosporine should be checked at each clinic visit. Other side eﬀects include gum hyperplasia, and hirsutism.

question: What term speciﬁcally describes the process, following protective immunization, in which antigen- responsive lymphocytes rapidly divide to increase their population?
explanation: To develop immunologic memory following protective immunization, relatively rare antigen-speciﬁc lymphocytes must initially come into contact with the antigen and become stimulated. Following this initial response, antigen-responsive lymphocytes rapidly divide to increase their population in a process called clonal expansion, then migrate to other sites. In the absence of further antigenic stimulation, the lymphocytes return to a resting state but are no longer naive to the antigen. Antibody-class switching from the IgM of the initial response to IgG and other isotypes allows these smaller isotypes to be able to leak passively to a peripheral site in the event of re-exposure to the antigen. Memory also requires that lymphocytes follow a complex migratory pattern called homing, in which they pass from the circulation into various tissues, then return to the circulation via the lymphatics.

question: What therapeutic agent, used in the treatment of severe uveitis, permanently cross-links deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and has the highest risk of secondary malignancy?
explanation: Patients with uveitis/scleritis that is non-responsive to corticosteroids or that requires doses of corticosteroids too high for long-term use should be transitioned to steroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy (IMT). Antimetabolites such as methotrexate, azathioprine, and mycophenolate mofetil have been used successfully. Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent that permanently cross-links DNA. Although it is very eﬀective in controlling inﬂammation, there is a signiﬁcant risk of myelosuppression, secondary infections, and subsequent neoplasia. Of these agents, cyclophosphamide has the BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What disorder is most likely to cause a low-grade, unilateral, chronic, anterior uveitis and be associated with iris atrophy and transillumination defects?
explanation: Hallmark features of viral iridocyclitis include low-grade, chronic cells; diﬀuse, tiny keratic precipitates (KP) that do not remain within the Arlt triangle; iris atrophy; iris transillumination; and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) during active ﬂare-ups. A feature more speciﬁc to herpetic iridocyclitis is the presence of larger KP with overlying stromal edema secondary to the associated underlying endothelial dysfunction (ie, disciform keratitis). Although herpetic disease comes to mind in considering these examination ﬁndings, any viral iridocyclitis can present with these ﬁndings (except disciform keratitis, which is more speciﬁc to herpetic disease), although not as pronounced as when they occur with herpetic disease. HLA-B27–associated acute anterior uveitis (AAU) can present with large keratic precipitates, a dense and ﬁbrinous anterior chamber reaction with associated formation of posterior synechiae, and a hypopyon, but iris atrophy and transillumination are not typical of HLA- B27–associated disease. VKH typically presents with bilateral exudative retinal detachments. Upon resolution of these detachments, future ﬂare-ups do tend to present as low-grade anterior chamber reactions, but there is no associated iris atrophy or transillumination. Sarcoidosis can present anywhere in the eye and can produce nongranulomatous and granulomatous inﬂammation (although the disease itself is granulomatous in nature); however, it does not result in iris atrophy or transillumination. Retinal ischemia from phlebitis with inﬂammation creates a neovascular complex in the snowbank.

explanation: Pars planitis is an idiopathic form of intermediate uveitis. Men and women are aﬀected equally, and there is a bimodal age distribution (5- 15 years old, 20-40 years old). Approximately 80% of cases of pars planitis are bilateral, which can often be asymmetric in severity. In children, the initial presentation may consist of signiﬁcant anterior chamber inﬂammation accompanied by redness, photophobia, and discomfort. The onset in teenagers and young adults may be more insidious, with the presenting complaint generally being ﬂoaters. Ocular manifestations include anterior chamber inﬂammatory cells, vitreous cells, snowballs, and pars plana exudates. Inferior peripheral retinal phlebitis with retinal venous sheathing is common. With long- standing inﬂammation, macular edema often develops; this condition becomes chronic and refractory in approximately 10% of patients and is the major cause of vision loss. Ischemia from retinal phlebitis, combined with angiogenic stimuli from intraocular inﬂammation, can lead to neovascularization along the inferior snowbank in up to 10% of cases. These neovascular complexes can result in vitreous hemorrhages, more common in children than adults; they also may BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

What virus is associated with this condition? contract, leading to peripheral tractional and rhegmatogenous retinal detachments. In rare cases, the complexes evolve into secondary peripheral retinal vasoproliferative tumors—vascular masses with exudative retinopathy and minimally dilated vessels—years after the initial diagnosis. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments are rare but localized peripheral detachments (serous or tractional) that can occur in 4 –10 of patients with pars planitis. With chronicity, posterior synechiae and band keratopathy may also develop. Other possible causes of loss of vision include cataracts, epiretinal membrane, and vitreous opaciﬁcation. Over 75 of cases are bilateral, but the severity of disease may vary between the eyes. Patients often present complaining of a subacute onset of ﬂoaters. Examination often shows anterior cells, anterior vitreous cells, snowballs, snowbanks (exudate over pars plana and ora serrate), and peripheral retinal phlebitis with vessel sheathing. Neovascularization can develop along the snowbank and lead to vitreous hemorrhage and/or rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Approximately 10 of pars planitis cases have a self-limiting, benign course; 30 have a smoldering course with remissions and exacerbations; and 60 have a chronic course without exacerbations, and 30 have multiple exacerbations over time. Treatment starts with periocular steroids, usually injected in the sub- Tenon space. For refractory cases, cryotherapy or laser photocoagulation may be applied posterior to the snowbank. Pars plana vitrectomy and immunomodulators may also be helpful in refractory cases. Long-term complications of pars planitis include cystoid macular edema (most common [50 ]), cataract, band keratopathy, and glaucoma.

Molluscum contagiosum is a viral infection of the skin caused by a DNA poxvirus and generally occurs in children and immunocompromised patients. It is spread through direct contact or shared items such as clothing or towels. When it aﬀects the periocular skin, it may result in follicular conjunctivitis. Primary herpes simplex 1 virus can manifest as a grouped vesicular eruption around the periocular skin. Parvovirus B19 causes a childhood rash called ﬁfth disease, which is commonly called slapped cheek syndrome. Human papillomavirus 6 and 11 have been associated with conjunctival papillomas and verruca vulgaris (common wart).

question: Vitreous biopsy should be considered in cases of uveitis if what condition is suspected?
explanation: Primary intraocular lymphoma (also known as primary vitreoretinal lymphoma and previously known as reticulum cell sarcoma) masquerades as chronic uveitis in patients above the age of 50 (peak 75-84 years old). Lymphoma will frequently respond to topical or systemic corticosteroids, but it is often not until it recurs or becomes recalcitrant to steroid therapy that a neoplastic cause is entertained. The gold standard for diagnosing intraocular lymphoma is histologic conﬁrmation of atypical lymphocytes, which requires vitrectomy. Further studies that can be performed on the vitrectomy specimen for lymphoma include high IL-10 to IL-6 ratio (supportive only, not diagnostic), immunohistochemistry for lambda or kappa light chains, ﬂow cytometry (evaluating for a clonal population of B-cells or T-cells), and IgH gene or T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement to elucidate monoclonality that typify a neoplastic, lymphomatous process. A vitrectomy can be not only diagnostic, but also therapeutic in cases of lymphoma, as it can remove visually signiﬁcant vitritis. Vitreous biopsy can be negative in one-third of cases, so repeat vitrectomy/vitreous biopsy should be considered if high suspicion exists and the initial biopsy is negative.

question: What kind of scleritis is most likely to be associated with systemic disease that has high mortality?
explanation: Necrotizing scleritis is the most severe and destructive type of scleritis, and more likely to lead to vision loss. It is more frequently associated with systemic disease (approximately 50%-60% of cases), some being life-threatening systemic vasculitic diseases. Necrotizing scleritis more frequently aﬀects older individuals, and is more prevalent in women. Patients with necrotizing scleritis and who were not diagnosed timely suﬀered from mortality rates as high as 30%. Propionibacterium acnes.

question: Delayed endophthalmitis (> 6 weeks) following cataract surgery is commonly caused by what pathogen?
explanation: Propionibacterium acnes is well known to cause a delayed or chronic mild endophthalmitis, following cataract or neodymium yttrium-argon- garnet (Nd:YAG) laser surgery, that can be confused with a noninfectious uveitis. Often no hypopyon or pain is present. The lens capsule may show gray-white deposits indicative of P acnes growth. Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Bacillus cereus usually present acutely with typical signs of exogenous bacterial endophthalmitis such as pain, cells and ﬂare, hypopyon, and decreased vision.

question: A 34-year-old previously healthy woman has painless blurred vision OS for 10 days. question: What method of intraocular pressure control should be avoided in a patient with chronic anterior uveitis?

options.B: It inhibits calcineurin and interleukin-2 transcription to suppress T-cell functioning.
options.C: It inhibits purine synthesis and subsequent DNA synthesis, which suppress T- and B-cell functioning.
options.D: It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, inhibiting folic acid, purine production, and subsequently DNA synthesis

explanation: Azathioprine is a prodrug of mercaptopurine that inhibits purine synthesis and consequently DNA synthesis and cell replication (which suppresses T- and B-cell functioning). It is used for a wide range of autoimmune diseases including lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Behçet disease, inﬂammatory bowel disease, and many others. It can cause hepatotoxicity. Inﬂiximab (Remicade) is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits tumor necrosis factor alpha. It is used to treat a variety of autoimmune diseases including psoriasis, Crohn disease, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and ulcerative colitis. It can cause leukopenia and may cause tumors to become clinically apparent sooner. Methotrexate competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, which inhibits folic acid. Folic acid is required for purine production and DNA synthesis. Therefore, DNA synthesis is inhibited. It is used to treat cancer including breast cancer, leukemia, lymphoma, head and neck cancer, osteosarcoma, and bladder cancers. It is also used to treat autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, lupus, Crohn disease and psoriatic arthritis. It has a long track record of use, and it is taken by mouth or by subcutaneous injection once a week. It can cause liver toxicity. Cyclosporine binds to cyclophilin, which inhibits calcineurin and interleukin-2 transcription to suppress T-cell functioning. It is used for a variety of autoimmune diseases including psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, and many others. It is also used to suppress organ transplant rejection. It is taken by mouth daily. It can cause hirsutism, kidney dysfunction, and hypertension.

question: What would be an anticipated intraoperative complication in a 40- year-old man with Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis?
explanation: Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis (also termed Fuchs uveitis syndrome or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) is characterized by unilateral, diﬀuse, small, white, stellate keratic precipitates; cells in the anterior chamber and the anterior vitreous; and heterochromia due to diﬀuse iris stromal atrophy. It is thought to be associated with viral infections (cytomegalovirus [CMV], rubella) and in other cases with toxoplasmosis. Glaucoma and cataracts occur frequently. Aqueous misdirection is a rare complication. Abnormal bridging vessels may be present in the iridocorneal angle. These may bleed during the cataract surgery and may lead to hyphema (this bleeding occurrence is known as Amsler sign [or Amsler-Verrey sign]). Corneal edema is associated with Fuchs corneal dystrophy, not Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis.

question: What is a characteristic feature seen on gonioscopy of Fuchs uveitis syndrome?

options.A: peripheral anterior synechiae extending anterior to the Schwalbe line
options.B: abnormal blood vessels bridging the angle that may bleed during surgery
options.C: widening of the ciliary body band

explanation: Fuchs uveitis syndrome (sometimes called Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) is unilateral, and symptoms range from none to mild blurring and discomfort. Signs include diﬀuse stromal atrophy with a "moth-eaten appearance" of the iris; small white stellate keratic precipitates scattered diﬀusely over the endothelium; anterior chamber cell; no synechiae; and abnormal vessels bridging the angle on gonioscopy that may bleed during surgery, causing a hyphema, glaucoma, and cataract. Few cases require treatment of the inﬂammation, and macular edema is uncommon. Histological examination shows plasma cells in the ciliary body. The etiology remains unclear but has been associated with rubella, toxoplasmosis, and cytomegalovirus.

question: Progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN) syndrome is most commonly associated with what virus?
explanation: PORN syndrome is a variant of herpetic viral retinitis seen in HIV- infected patients. Initially, PORN may be diﬃcult to diﬀerentiate from CMV retinitis, but rapid progression distinguishes varicella-zoster or herpes simplex from CMV infections. Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis can mimic PORN in AIDS patients, and vitreous polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is often required to diﬀerentiate the possible etiologies. Bartonella species may cause bacillary angiomatosis or neuroretinitis but are not associated with a peripheral retinitis. The human papillomavirus (HPV) is associated with cervical and squamous carcinoma but has no known association with retinitis.

question: What is a contraindication to cataract surgery in a patient with uveitis?
explanation: The decision to perform cataract surgery in patients with uveitic eyes diﬀers from considering this surgery for patients with nonuveitic eyes. The potential vision may be subnormal, due to previous macular edema or other permanent ocular damage. Active intraocular inﬂammation is a strong contraindication for surgery and should only be considered if the risks of delaying surgery outweigh the potential for dramatically exacerbating the inﬂammation. Complications can be minimized when inﬂammation has been controlled for several months before surgery and is treated aggressively after surgery. Steroid-responsive glaucoma is not a contraindication for cataract surgery but should be considered when weighing the relative merits of periocular or intraocular corticosteroid use. Many uveitis patients require systemic immunomodulatory therapy to obtain the necessary control of the inﬂammatory process before cataract surgery; the ideal scenario is absence of inﬂammatory cells, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the typical ophthalmoscopic ﬁnding in multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis?

options.A: geographic chorioretinal pigmented scars radiating from the optic nerve
options.B: small white choroidal lesions (200- 500 µm) that resolve spontaneously over 4-8 weeks
options.C: choroidal inﬁltrates larger than 1 disc diameter
options.D: small creamy lesions acutely that become punched out over time

explanation: The inﬂammatory lesions in multifocal choroiditis may vary somewhat in number, appearance, and location, but they are rarely larger than 1500 μm, evolve into punched-out atrophic scars, and are associated BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: In a patient with sympathetic ophthalmia, what feature is classically found in the sympathizing eye on examination?
explanation: Dalen-Fuchs nodules, which are multifocal inﬁltrates at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) are typically seen in the sympathizing eye. Hollenhorst plaques are cholesterol emboli that are not associated with sympathetic ophthalmia. In sympathetic ophthalmia, inﬂammation typically involves the uveal tissue, and retinal inﬁltrates are not a feature. Elschnig spots are seen in hypertensive choroidopathy.

question: An ophthalmologist suspects that a patient has intraocular inﬂammation related to toxoplasmosis and decides to perform a Goldmann-Witmer test. What 2 tissue samples are needed to perform this test?
explanation: The Goldmann-Witmer (GW) coeﬃcient for a speciﬁc pathogen is calculated by dividing the amount of IgG reactive to a speciﬁc pathogen (xIgG) in aqueous by the total amount of IgG in the aqueous, and then dividing that ratio by a ratio created by dividing the amount of the same speciﬁc antigen IgG (xIgG) in serum by the total amount of IgG in serum: GW = (xIgG in aqueous/total IgG in aqueous)/(xIgG in serum/total IgG in serum)

question: For patients with punctate inner choroidopathy (PIC), what is the most common cause for decreased visual acuity?
explanation: Serpiginous choroiditis, multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis (MCP), and PIC all may have visual morbidity secondary to subfoveal and submacular CNVMs. Of these 3 disease entities, PIC has the highest incidence of CNVM at presentation (up to 79%), with subsequent permanent vision loss. However, MCP tends to have a worse visual outcome overall.

question: What are the only cells to constitutively express major histocompatibility (MHC) class II molecules in the conjunctiva and limbus?
explanation: Langerhans cells are a subset of dendritic cells that are present in most human epithelial cells. Their main function is acting as accessory immunoregulatory cells that process and present antigens to T lymphocytes through the MCH class II molecule. By presenting the processed antigens, Langerhans cells activate and initiate responses BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient with uveitis has urethritis and oral ulcers. Given the anterior and posterior ﬁndings shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The anterior segment ﬁnding of posterior synechiae may be found in any of the uveitic conditions listed. However, the posterior segment ﬁnding of retinal vasculitis (sheathing of the vessels) that involves both arterioles and venules is consistent with Adamantiades-Behçet Disease (ABD). Additionally, the systemic ﬁndings of urethritis and oral ulcers are typical of the nonocular features of ABD. While syphilis can masquerade as a noninfectious uveitis, urethritis and oral ulcers are not typical for infection. Rather, a painless chancre at the site of inoculation (for example, genitalia) can be seen in primary syphilis. TINU can feature posterior synechiae, but retinal vasculitis is not seen. The nephritis seen in TINU is not characterized by urethritis. Instead, there can be white cell casts, protein, eosinophils, and blood found on urinalysis with microscopy. VKH does not feature urethritis or oral ulcers. Additionally, retinal vasculitis is not seen in VKH.

question: Over the last 3 months, a 53-year- old woman has developed occasional headaches and intermittent left eye pain and blurring. Her only medication is oral doxycycline for rosacea. Her visual acuity is 20/20 on the right and 20/40 on the left, and her color vision, pupillary reactions, and slit- lamp examination are normal OU. She has metamorphopsia on Amsler grid testing in the left eye. Given her fundus appearance shown, what is her most likely diagnosis?
What is the deﬁnitive treatment for a patient with phacolytic uveitis?

options.A: topical prednisolone acetate drops given hourly
options.B: oral methotrexate following baseline hepatic function tests

question: A 30-year-old woman presents with blurred vision and photopsias that started in her right eye, then aﬀected her left eye also. She had a fever, malaise, and headache one week ago. Her fundus appearance is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)

question: The activation of what cell type characterizes the anamnestic response to secondary antigen stimulation in adaptive immunity?

A patient presents with acute anterior uveitis and decreased vision. The patient denies pain with eye movements. Pupillary function is normal without aﬀerent pupillary defect. Color plates are full. Anterior segment ﬁndings include 2+ diﬀuse perilimbal injection, 3+ anterior chamber cell, 1+ ﬂare, and a clear crystalline lens. Dilated fundoscopic examination shows hyperemia of the optic nerve and a blunted foveal reﬂex, but no vitritis or chorioretinal lesions. What test would most likely demonstrate the cause of decreased vision in this case?

options.B: optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve
options.C: B-scan ultrasonography of the optic nerve
options.D: optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula

explanation: The cause of the patient's decreased vision would best be discerned through OCT of the macula, as it is not uncommon for inﬂammatory cytokines associated with acute anterior uveitis to diﬀuse posteriorly and result in swelling of the optic nerve head and in cystoid macular edema (CME). It is important to understand that the presence of optic nerve and retinal edema alone are not synonymous with posterior uveitis or optic neuritis. Optic nerve and retinal edema occur in many processes including anterior uveitis, intermediate uveitis, posterior uveitis, panuveitis. Edema can also occur in unrelated entities such as hypotony maculopathy in the setting of an overﬁltering bleb in glaucoma patients. To further clarify that the optic nerve head hyperemia in this patient is not indicative of an optic neuritis or posterior uveitis, the question stem not only states that this is an acute anterior uveitis, but also explains that there is no pain with eye movements, no vitritis, no chorioretinitis, no aﬀerent pupillary defect, and full color plate testing. Another option to ensure that optic nerve function is normal could be to perform a visual ﬁeld, which should either be full in the absence of other pathology or show a possible enlarged blind spot from the edema at the nerve head. Therefore, OCT and/or B-scan ultrasonography of the optic nerve head will not be as helpful in this scenario, as there is no reason to suspect an optic neuritis or posterior scleritis with associated optic nerve swelling in this case. ERG may be helpful in conditions primarily involving the retina or choroid, such as certain white dot syndromes or birdshot retinochoroidopathy, but not in the setting of acute anterior uveitis where optic nerve head edema and macular edema can result from posterior diﬀusion of inﬂammatory cytokines.

question: What is the most serious manifestation associated with acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)?
explanation: Cerebral vasculitis can result in infarction in areas of the brain, which can eventually lead to stroke or death. Thus, cerebral vasculitis (which is a systemic condition associated with APMPPE) is the most serious manifestation of APMPPE. Optic nerve edema in APMPPE resolves with resolution of the placoid lesions. A viral prodrome can be ascertained upon review of a patient's history. CNV can be seen rarely in APMPPE as well, but the condition is not as serious as cerebral vasculitis.

question: For an AIDS patient that has the fundus ﬁndings shown, what is the most likely symptom that he might experience?
explanation: The image represents peripheral "granular" cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. Typical features include minimal or no vitreous inﬂammation, preservation of the vessels (although varying amounts of vasculitis/sheathing may be present), and steady progression without treatment. Because the lesions are usually peripheral and the host immune response is compromised, signs or symptoms such as pain, redness, and decreased vision are scarce; thus, routine screening ophthalmoscopy is recommended for those with CD4 T-cell counts below 250 cells/μL. +.

question: What posterior uveitis disorder can present with marked visual symptoms but minimal ﬁndings on clinical exam?
explanation: Acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR) can present with numerous visual complaints but very minimal funduscopic changes; however, patients can have marked abnormalities on electroretinography (ERG), multifocal ERG, and visual ﬁeld testing. The condition can even be misdiagnosed as functional vision loss if no additional testing is performed. Fundus pigment changes often appear in the later stages of the disease and can be more apparent on ﬂuorescein angiography or fundus autoﬂuorescence. Serpiginous choroiditis and PIC present with characteristic scars and foci of localized inﬂammation. Although the prodromal phase of Vogt- Koyanagi-Harada syndrome can have minimal ocular ﬁndings, patients have typical systemic symptoms and by the time they present with vision loss, they have panuveitis and exudative retinal detachments.

question: What osteoporosis therapy is most strongly implicated as a cause of ocular inﬂammatory disease?
explanation: Bisphosphonates (such as alendronate, etidronate, risedronate, and zoledronic acid) have been associated with the development of uveitis. Other medications that have been associated with uveitis include oral contraceptives, rifabutin, sulfonamides, diethylcarbamazine, etanercept, topical metipranolol, topical prostaglandin analogues (PGAs), intravitreal cidofovir, and intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections.

question: Ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, inﬂammatory bowel disease, and psoriatic arthritis are all strongly associated with anterior uveitis and what serum marker?
explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, inﬂammatory bowel disease, and psoriatic arthritis are the seronegative spondyloarthropathies. They are strongly associated with anterior uveitis and HLA-B27 positivity. By deﬁnition ("seronegative"), patients with these conditions are negative for rheumatoid factor. HLA-A29 is associated with birdshot chorioretinopathy, whereas ANCA is often positive in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

question: What is a helpful diagnostic characteristic of multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (shown)?
explanation: Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome is usually unilateral. It is most common in young females, not males. The tempo of onset is typically rapid or explosive. The associated peripapillary, central, or cecocentral scotomata usually resolve over several weeks. Recurrence is uncommon. 2 50 per pag.

question: What test is indicated periodically in patients being treated with azathioprine for eye disease with no systemic symptoms?
explanation: Azathioprine is an oral antimetabolite that is often used to treat ocular inﬂammatory diseases, such as uveitis and mucous membrane pemphigoid. Hepatotoxicity and blood cell dyscrasias are the most common adverse eﬀects that would be detected by screening laboratory studies; thus, most surveillance regimens include getting a complete blood cell count. Liver enzymes, such as ALT, should be checked before initiating therapy, within 1 to 2 weeks after initiating therapy, and regularly thereafter. Use of the alkylating agent cyclophosphamide can result in hemorrhagic cystitis. Consumption of adequate water is therefore recommended when taking this drug, and urinalysis is indicated.

question: What therapy would be contraindicated in a patient with multiple sclerosis-associated uveitis?
explanation: TNF-alpha inhibitors have been implicated in the appearance of demyelinating lesions. As such, these agents should be avoided in patients with MS to avoid exacerbation of their underlying demyelinating disease. Furthermore, it is important to consider the possibility of MS in patients BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: In what setting is the use of tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha inhibitors contraindicated?

options.B: anterior uveitis associated with HLA- B27
options.C: posterior uveitis in a child younger than 10 years old
options.D: intermediate uveitis associated with periventricular T2 changes on cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

explanation: TNF-alpha inhibitors are approved for the treatment of noninfectious uveitis. The use of TNF-alpha inhibitors is associated with worsening on demyelinating lesions in the brain and should not be used in patients BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) in patients with uveitis is characterized by what feature?

options.A: a relatively low association with panuveitis
options.B: a relatively high association with retinal dialysis
options.C: a relatively low association with infectious uveitis
options.D: a relatively high association with proliferative vitreoretinopathy

explanation: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment occurs in 3% of patients with uveitis. Panuveitis and infectious uveitis are the entities most commonly associated with RRD. Up to 30% of patients may have BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What type of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is associated with the highest risk for uveitis?
explanation: Anterior uveitis can be associated with all forms of JIA. Oligoarticular onset (previously known as pauciarticular onset) JIA accounts for 80%-90% of patients with JIA-associated uveitis. Four or fewer joints are involved during the ﬁrst 6 months of disease. The severity, onset, and exacerbations of uveitis can be diﬀerent from the joint disease; that is, severe anterior uveitis can occur with mild arthritis as well as before or after the arthritis. Nevertheless, it should be noted that no matter how severe the anterior uveitis, it is asymptomatic in nature, and therefore it is crucial for children diagnosed with JIA to be screened for ocular involvement.

question: A patient is suspected to have Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis after cataract surgery. What antibiotic is recommended for vitreous injection?
explanation: The intravitreal or endocapsular antibiotic that is appropriate for the treatment of P acnes (a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus) is vancomycin. P acnes endophthalmitis often presents with mild inﬂammation postoperatively, and the hallmark feature is a whitish intracapsular plaque (or plaques). Suspicion can be conﬁrmed with Gram stain and/or anaerobic cultures, which should be held for at least 2 weeks because P acnes is a slow-growing organism. Although intravitreal or endocapsular injection of vancomycin may initially help, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What test is an indicator of active infection in syphilis disease?

options.A: microhemagglutination assay for T pallidum antibodies (MHA-TP)

explanation: The serum rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test can be an indicator of active syphilitic infection but does not conﬁrm that a patient has syphilis; for that, a treponemal test, such as the ﬂuorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) assay and the microhemagglutination assay for T pallidum antibodies (MHA-TP) is needed. FTA-ABS and MHA-TP are BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the most likely ocular ﬁnding in a neonate with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS)?
explanation: A unilateral or bilateral pigmentary retinopathy is the most common ocular manifestation of CRS (25%–50%), followed by cataract (15%) and glaucoma (10%). The pigmentary disturbance, often described as “salt-and-pepper” fundus, shows considerable variation, ranging from ﬁnely stippled, bone spicule–like, small, black, irregular masses to gross pigmentary irregularities with coarse, blotchy mottling. It can be stationary or progressive. Despite loss of the foveal light reﬂex and prominent pigmentary changes, neither vision nor electroretinogram results are typically aﬀected. Congenital (nuclear) cataracts and BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What pathologic ﬁnding characterizes lens-induced uveitis after trauma?

options.C: asteroid bodies within lens epithelial cells

question: A 4-year-old is referred for unilateral hypopyon. Perinatal history is unremarkable, and there is no signiﬁcant family history. Systemic workup for infectious and inﬂammatory disorders is noncontributory. What should be the next step? Histologically, a zonal granulomatous inﬂammation is found at the site of lens injury. Neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, epithelioid cells, and giant cells may be seen. Uveitis may result from an immune reaction to lens material. This may occur after trauma or surgery associated with disruption of the lens capsule or from leakage of lens proteins through the lens capsule in mature or hypermature cataracts (phacolysis). Speciﬁcally, phacolytic uveitis (or phacolytic glaucoma, as it is frequently termed) involves an acute increase in intraocular pressure (IOP) caused by clogging of the trabecular meshwork by macrophages engorged with lens proteins leaking through the intact capsule of a hypermature cataract. Juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG) is a benign proliferative disorder of histiocytic cells of the dermal dendrocyte phenotype. JXG belongs to the broad group of non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses and is typically a disorder of early childhood. JXG presents in the ﬁrst 2 years of life as a solitary reddish or yellowish skin papule or nodule. Ocular lesions can involve the eyelids or iris. Histologically, JXG is characterized by the presence of foamy or Touton giant cells. Asteroid bodies are star-shaped, acidophilic bodies found within the multinucleated giant cells of sarcoidosis.

options.B: pars plana needle biopsy for ﬂow cytometry
options.C: examination under anesthesia with ultrasonography imaging

explanation: Hypopyon and uveitis in the pediatric population is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise. The diagnosis of retinoblastoma can usually be made during a dilated indirect ophthalmoscopic examination performed under anesthesia; the characteristic ﬁnding is a chalky, oﬀ-white retinal mass with a soft, friable consistency. Ocular ultrasonography shows a solid intraocular tumor with characteristic intratumoral calciﬁcations. CT scan is not recommended in patients with suspected retinoblastoma, because there is a risk of radiation-induced secondary cancers in patients with germinal disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be helpful to conﬁrm the presence of an intraocular mass. Sixty (60) percent of children with retinoblastoma have the unilateral, non-germline, and non-heritable form of the disease. In cases of unilateral disease, molecular/genetic testing should be done initially on tumor cells (if available from enucleation) to identify the speciﬁc RB1 mutation. It is not indicated in the initial work up for diagnosis. Needle biopsy is contraindicated in retinoblastoma, as seeding of the tumor can occur.

question: What is the most common cause of vision loss in pars planitis?
explanation: Pars planitis refers to intermediate uveitis that is idiopathic. Cystoid macular edema is the number one cause of vision loss in pars planitis and can be chronic and refractory in up to 10% of patients. Other causes of vision loss in pars planitis include cataract, epiretinal membrane, and vitreous opaciﬁcation. Vitreous hemorrhage can occur due to neovascularization in the peripheral retina but is not a common cause of vision loss. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments can occur but are less common than serous or tractional detachments. Pars plana exudates, or snowbanks, can be seen in pars planitis and may indicate a more severe course, but they are not a major cause of vision loss.

question: How does bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) activate the immune system?
explanation: Bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is an intrinsic component of the cell walls of most gram-negative bacteria. It is one of the most important molecules that trigger the innate immune response. Plasma cell induction, the formation of antibodies, and establishing memory B cells are all part of the more pathogen-speciﬁc, targeted, and slower adaptive immune response.

question: What is the most common cause of vision loss due to ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS)?
explanation: The most common cause of vision loss in OHS is CNV. If 1 eye with OHS has CNV, then the risk that the other eye will develop visual loss is 1% if there are no ﬁndings of OHS in the fellow eye; 4% if there is peripapillary atrophy in the fellow eye; and 25% if focal macular histo spots are present. The treatment of CNV in OHS includes photodynamic therapy or anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti- VEGF) therapy. Inﬂammatory vitreous opacities and retinal vasculitis are absent in OHS. The classic peripheral punched-out chorioretinal scars of OHS typically do not cause vision loss.

question: What is the typical pattern of chorioretinitis in West Nile virus?

options.A: optic nerve edema with star-shaped macular exudate
options.B: linear groups of chorioretinal scars along the nerve ﬁber layer
options.C: arteriolar attenuation and diﬀuse retinal pigment epithelial mottling
options.D: large, ﬂat placoid lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium

explanation: Ocular manifestations of West Nile virus include pain, photophobia, blurred vision, and conjunctival hyperemia. A characteristic multifocal chorioretinitis is present in most patients. The chorioretinal lesions vary in size and number and present in distinctive linear arrays following the course of retinal nerve ﬁber layer. Fundoscopic examination in acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) demonstrates large, ﬂat, yellow-white placoid lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium that are scattered throughout the posterior pole. Neuroretinitis, characterized by vision loss, optic nerve swelling, and macular star formation, can be caused by Bartonella henselae (cat- scratch disease). The fundus may initially appear normal in autoimmune retinopathy, but arteriolar attenuation, retinal pigment epithelial mottling, and diﬀuse retinal and optic nerve atrophy may develop as the disease progresses.

question: What uveitic condition is (weakly) associated with HLA-DR4?
explanation: HLA-DR4 has been weakly associated with both Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome and sympathetic ophthalmia. anterior uveitis.

question: What is the most common ocular presentation of cytomegalovirus (CMV) in an immunocompetent patient?
explanation: The most common ocular manifestations of CMV immunocompetent individuals are anterior uveitis, subepithelial inﬁltrates, and endotheliitis, either individually or in combination. In adults, the anterior uveitis may be associated with ocular hypertension, corneal edema, and sectoral iris atrophy. The most common ocular manifestation of CMV in immunocompromised patients is posterior segment disease (ie, CMV retinitis).

question: A patient presents with large keratic precipitates, posterior synechiae, and vitritis. A puriﬁed protein derivative (PPD) test is placed as part of the workup and is read 48 hours later at 6 mm induration. Under what condition would this PPD be considered positive?

options.A: The patient has a history of intravenous drug abuse.
options.C: The patient had contact with an individual with active tuberculosis.
options.D: The patient is a healthcare worker.

explanation: An induration of at least 5 mm is considered positive in those exposed to active tuberculosis, those with HIV infection, or in patients with radiographic evidence of healed tuberculous lesions. An induration of 10 mm or more is considered positive in high-risk groups, which include patients with diabetes, those with renal failure, those on systemic immunomodulatory therapy, immigrants from TB-endemic areas, and health care workers. In this scenario, the PPD from the patient with an induration of 6 mm and recent contact with a person with active TB would be considered positive.

question: A sewer-system worker from Puerto Rico presents with uveitis-associated hypopyon. For what infection is this patient at particularly increased risk?
explanation: Although the natural reservoirs for Leptospira interrogans are animals, humans can become infected with this zoonotic organism, especially when their jobs place them in contact with an infected animal's urine. Thus, sewer workers, veterinarians, and farmers are at higher risk for this infection. Interestingly, half of the cases identiﬁed in the US occur in Puerto Rico. Tularemia (caused by Francisella tularensis) is acquired from the bites of ticks and deerﬂies, as well as from rabbits. In brucellosis, contact with dogs, pigs, goats and meat, placentas, or milk from infected cows leads to acquiring Brucella. Meat packers, veterinarians, or farm hands would be the employees most aﬀected. Because the etiologic agent of onchocerciasis (river blindness) is the larva of Onchocerca volvulus, which is transmitted through the bite of a female black ﬂy endemic to sub-Saharan Africa, a patient from that region would be most likely to have this parasitic infection.

question: On the previous examination, a patient had the fundus appearance shown below. The patient presents at the current examination with a mild decrease in vision. What would be an indication for a course of systemic therapy with antimicrobials and corticosteroids?

options.C: peripheral retinitis and overlying mild vitritis
options.D: cells in the anterior chamber and elevated intraocular pressure

question: A patient with panuveitis secondary to Behçet disease recently started inﬂiximab infusions. What medication can be given to decrease the risk of drug-induced lupus? Toxoplasma gondii chorioretinitis is typically due to a reactivation of latent disease. The disease can be acquired transplacentally (as one of the congenital TORCH infections) or after birth, upon exposure to cysts in soil, food, or cat feces. Many episodes are self-limited and do not require therapy. Indications for treatment include an immunocompromised patient, dense vitreous opacity, large lesions greater than 1 disc diameter in size, multiple lesions, decreased visual acuity, frequent recurrences, or retinitis threatening the optic nerve or macula. Milder vitritis and peripheral retinitis do not necessarily require treatment; however, some experts suggest prophylactic therapy for patients with frequently recurrent disease. Findings can include anterior chamber reaction and intraocular pressure elevation, but these do not necessitate antimicrobial and steroid treatment. The classic regimen for the treatment of ocular toxoplasmosis consists of triple therapy: pyrimethamine (loading dose, 50–100 mg; treatment dose, 25–50 mg/day), sulfadiazine (treatment dose, 1 g, 4 times/day), and prednisone (treatment dose, 0.5–1 mg/kg/day, depending on the severity of the inﬂammation). Because sulfonamides and pyrimethamine inhibit folic acid metabolism, folinic acid (15 mg every day) is added to prevent myelosuppression (leukopenia and/or thrombocytopenia), which may result from pyrimethamine therapy. Systemic corticosteroids are generally begun either at the time of antimicrobial therapy or within 48 hours in immunocompetent patients. question: What mechanism dominates the inﬂammatory eﬀector response in sympathetic ophthalmia?
explanation: The eﬀector responses of immunity can be divided into 3 main categories: antibody-mediated eﬀector responses, lymphocyte- mediated eﬀector responses (delayed hypersensitivity {DH}, cytotoxic lymphocytes), and combined antibody and cellular mechanisms. Delayed hypersensitivity (previously termed Coombs and Gell type IV) represents the prototypical adaptive immune mechanism for lymphocyte-triggered inﬂammation. It is especially powerful in secondary immune responses. Previously primed DH CD4+ T lymphocytes leave the lymph node, home into local tissues where antigen persists, and become activated by restimulation with the speciﬁc priming antigen and major histocompatibility (MHC) class II– expressing antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Fully activated DH T lymphocytes secrete mediators and cytokines, leading to the recruitment and activation of macrophages and/or other nonspeciﬁc leukocytes. The term delayed for this type of hypersensitivity refers to the fact that the reaction becomes maximal 12–48 hours after antigen exposure. One of the most important determinants of the pattern of DH reaction is the subtype of DH CD4+ eﬀector T cells that mediate the reaction. Just as helper T lymphocytes can be diﬀerentiated into 3 groups—Th1, Th2, and Th17 subsets—according to the spectrum of cytokines secreted, DH T lymphocytes can also be grouped by the same criteria. Th1 subset of cytokines, especially IFN-γ (also known as macrophage- activating factor) and tumor necrosis factor-beta (TNF-β), activates macrophages to secrete inﬂammatory mediators and kill pathogens, thus amplifying inﬂammation. Th2-mediated DH mechanisms are thought to play a major role in the following: response to parasite infections, late-phase responses of allergic reactions, asthma, atopic dermatitis, or other manifestations of atopic diseases. Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral panuveitis that follows penetrating trauma to an eye. It is unclear whether the injury causes a de novo primary immunization to self-antigens or if the injury instead somehow changes the immunologic microenvironment of the retina, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and uvea so that a secondary aﬀerent response is initiated that serves to alter preexisting tolerance to retinal and uveal self-antigens. The inﬂammatory eﬀector response is thought to be dominated by a Th1-mediated DH mechanism generated in response to uveal or retinal antigens. CD4+ T lymphocytes predominate early in the disease course, although CD8+ T lymphocytes can be numerous in chronic cases. Activated macrophages are also numerous in granulomas, and Th1 cytokines have been identiﬁed in the vitreous or produced by T lymphocytes recovered from the eyes of aﬀected patients.

explanation: When diagnostic workup, as in the case of sight-threatening chorioretinitis, fails to reveal a diagnosis or, at the very least distinguish between noninfectious, infectious, or masquerade (eg, malignant) etiologies, a chorioretinal biopsy can be considered, since this will biopsy the tissue directly involved. question: What type of immunity provides immediate protection and requires no prior contact with the foreign substance or organism?
explanation: An immune response is a sequence of molecular and cellular events intended to rid the host of a threat: oﬀending pathogenic organisms, toxic substances, cellular debris, or neoplastic cells. There are 2 broad categories of immune responses, innate and adaptive. Innate immune responses, or natural immunity, require no prior contact with or “education” about the stimulus against which they are directed. Adaptive (or acquired) responses are higher-order, more speciﬁc responses directed against unique antigens. The adaptive immune response has 2 arms/compartments that closely interact with each other: one of humoral defense, employing soluble antibodies secreted by plasma cells, and another of cell-mediated defense, coordinated by T lymphocytes.

explanation: Cytokines Cytokines are soluble polypeptide mediators synthesized and released by cells for the purposes of intercellular signaling and communication. Paracrine Paracrine signaling refers to signaling of neighboring cells at the same site. Autocrine Autocrine signaling refers to stimulation of a receptor on its own cell surface. Endocrine Endocrine signaling refers to action on a distant site through release into the blood. Other similar sounding terms include apocrine, eccrine and holocrine. Apocrine Apocrine secretion refers to secretions containing the apical part of the secreting cells (decapitation secretion), eccrine eccrine secretion refers to secretion without loss of any part of the secreting cells (eg, sweat and tears), and holocrine holocrine secretion refers to secretions from sebaceous glands where the secretion contains the entire secreting cell.

question: In contrast to other white dot syndromes, what feature is invariably absent in punctate inner choroiditis (PIC)?
explanation: Punctate inner choroiditis/choroidopathy (PIC) is classically a disease of young myopic females that is most commonly bilateral, although the ﬁndings may be asymmetric. It is characterized by small white-yellow chorioretinal lesions (100-200 μm) that rarely extend to the midperiphery. In contrast to other white dot syndromes, which typically have variable degrees of vitritis, these lesions are never associated with vitritis. These lesions can be accompanied by decreased visual acuity as well as central or paracentral scotomas. Choroidal neovascularization is a common complication that can threaten visual outcomes.

question: A 24-year-old man from India presents with the ﬁnding in the photograph. He has similar ﬁndings in the other eye. The macula and optic nerves of both eyes were normal appearing. Laboratory tests show a normal fasting blood sugar, normal serum angiotensin converting enzyme, nonreactive rapid plasma reagin (RPR), negative antinuclear antibody (ANA), negative serum toxoplasmosis antibody, negative Lyme Western- blot, unremarkable chest x-ray, negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), and negative sickle screen.
