explanation: Eales disease is a primary occlusive retinopathy with unknown cause. It usually presents in men aged 20-30 years, more commonly in those from India and the Middle East. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and is characterized by bilateral idiopathic retinal perivasculitis with peripheral nonperfusion and neovascularization. A sea-fan of peripheral neovascularization may be seen. Vascular sheathing is seen in about 80% of patients, and both arteries and veins may be involved. All patients have conﬂuent peripheral nonperfusion with a sharply demarcated border between perfused and non-perfused peripheral retina. Neovascularization is typically seen at this border and is most commonly found in the temporal quadrant. Vitreous hemorrhage is the most common reason for visual loss, and traction retinal detachments may develop. Treatment is with laser photocoagulation to areas of nonperfused retina. Eales disease has been associated with tuberculin hypersensitivity. Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV) is an acquired abnormal choroidal vasculopathy (variant of age-related macular degeneration) that clinically presents as hemorrhagic detachments of the pigment epithelium and neurosensory retina. PCV occurs more commonly in persons with darkly pigmented skin, although persons with lighter pigmentation can be aﬀected as well. PCV typically occurs in the peripapillary or macular region although the periphery can be aﬀected as well. The utilization of indocyanine green (ICG) angiography can be helpful in making the diagnosis and visualizing abnormalities within the choroidal vasculature. Management can include observation, photodynamic therapy, anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti- VEGF) intravitreal injections, and rarely surgery. Coats disease is a sporadic condition that is typically unilateral and has a male predominance (85%). Chromosome 4 has been implicated as the site of the gene involved. Findings include retinal telangiectasia (vascular dilatation) including microaneurysms, fusiform capillary dilatation, venous dilatation, and ectatic arterioles. The vessels are compromised and leak ﬂuid that may cause exudative retinal detachment. Retinal exudates range from minimal to widespread.

A patient presents with increased ﬂoaters (see fundus photo). Her primary care physician is concerned about sarcoidosis, based on her review of symptoms. What is the most sensitive radiologic test to conﬁrm the physician's suspicion?
explanation: Sarcoidosis can frequently present as an intermediate uveitis characterized by snowballs, string of pearl vitreous opacities, and vitreous cells. In the United States, sarcoidosis should be suspected as a cause of intermediate uveitis, and high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest is more sensitive than chest x-ray at identifying hilar adenopathy, pulmonary nodules, and interstitial ﬁbrosis that may characterize pulmonary involvement in this disease. Central nervous system involvement by sarcoidosis is very variable, making chest imaging the more sensitive test. Gallium scanning has been used to check for occult disease activity, but it has limited sensitivity. Fluorine-18-ﬂuorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography is considered more accurate in pulmonary and extra-pulmonary sarcoidosis, but its utility in ophthalmic sarcoidosis is not well deﬁned. The ﬁnding of mononuclear alveolitis with increased CD4+ lymphocytes, as revealed by bronchoalveolar lavage, can also help support the diagnosis.

question: A 42-year-old White man presents with 2 days of malaise and rapidly progressive vision loss in the right eye. He is HIV positive with a CD4 count of 5 cells/mm3. Visual acuity is 20/100 right eye and 20/25 left eye. Dilated fundus examination of both eyes is shown in the ﬁgures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has Cryptococcus neoformans, which is a budding yeast and a common cause of fungal endophthalmitis in AIDS patients. Frequently patients present with a concurrent cryptococcal meningitis. However, retinal lesions may be present without or prior to meningeal symptoms. The most common ocular presentation is with yellowish- white fundus lesions of various sizes. Vitritis and keratic precipitates may also be present. The patient should have a lumbar puncture, and treatment is with intravenous amphotericin. Multifocal choroiditis is an inﬂammatory condition with lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choriocapillaris. This disease typically aﬀects women 20-60 years old, is bilateral, and presents with a vitritis and multiple yellow choroidal lesions that develop into chorioretinal scars similar to histoplasmosis. Macular edema and choroidal neovascularization are complications. Corticosteroids are used to control inﬂammation. Multifocal choroiditis is a diagnosis of exclusion and ruling out infectious causes is a must. In this question, the history of HIV positivity with a low CD4 cell count is more likely to be infectious than inﬂammatory. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that has predilection for more darkly pigmented ethnic groups, including persons of Asian, Hispanic, Native American, and Middle Eastern ancestry. Patients usually have a prodromal phase of a ﬂu-like illness. A uveitic phase follows, with bilateral panuveitis, exudate, and serous retinal detachment. In later phases, the fundus may develop a "sunset glow" with Dalen-Fuchs nodules. Cataract, glaucoma, and choroidal neovascularization are complications. Dermatologic manifestations include vitiligo, poliosis, alopecia, and the Sugiura sign, which is perilimbal vitiligo. Treatment is with corticosteroids and visual prognosis is usually good. The most common fungal endophthalmitis is Candida. Patients at risk include those who are immunocompromised, with indwelling catheters, chronic antibiotic use, hyperalimentation, or diabetes mellitus. Patients present with single or multiple yellow-white choroidal lesions with mild to moderate inﬂammation. Subretinal lesions may break through the retina into the vitreous. Vitreous inﬁltrates often have a "string of pearls" conﬁguration. Intravenous amphotericin B is adequate for treatment of choroidal lesions, but ﬂuconazole is better for treatment of vitreous lesions. Intravitreal or systemic voriconazole can also be used. question: A 25-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of vision loss in the right eye. He states that he is HIV positive, with a CD4 count of 44 cells/μL. His visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye and count ﬁngers at 3 feet in the right eye. The examination of the left eye is unremarkable. Fundus examination of the right eye is shown in the ﬁgure. explanation: The ﬁgure depicts cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis in an HIV-positive patient. CMV retinitis is the most common ocular opportunistic infection in patients with AIDS (and is an AIDS-deﬁning illness). However, over the past 2 decades since the introduction of modern antiretroviral therapy, the prevalence of CMV retinitis has decreased dramatically. CMV retinitis usually occurs when CD4 count drops below 50 cells/μL. Patients present with blurry vision and/or ﬂoaters. Clinically, the retina appears white and may have intraretinal hemorrhage, exudate, necrosis, periphlebitis, or "frosted-branch" angiitis. Vitritis may or may not be present, and when present it is usually mild. Retinal detachment occurs in up to half of the patients. Laser photocoagulation and pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade are frequently used to try to control or prevent retinal detachment, with variable success. Options for systemic coverage include high-dose induction with either intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg twice daily) or foscarnet (90 mg/kg twice daily) for 2 weeks, followed by low-dose daily maintenance therapy or oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily) for 3 weeks, followed by maintenance therapy (900 mg/day). Then patients may be switched to oral ganciclovir if they clinically improve. If patients do not improve, a ganciclovir intravitreal implant can be used. Oral valganciclovir 900 mg twice per day for 3 weeks is another acceptable induction therapy, if intravenous therapy is not desired. Intravitreal ganciclovir and foscarnet have been used oﬀ-label as well. Myelosuppression is a known side eﬀect of systemic ganciclovir. + BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

What type of macrophage contributes to ﬁbrosis, wound healing, and angiogenesis?
explanation: Resting macrophages are the classic scavenging cell, capable of phagocytosis and uptake of dead cell membranes, chemically modiﬁed extracellular protein (ie, acetylated or oxidized lipoproteins), sugar ligands, naked nucleic acids, and bacterial pathogens. Resting monocytes express at least 3 types of scavenging receptors but synthesize very low levels of proinﬂammatory cytokines. Scavenging can occur in the absence of inﬂammation. Primed macrophages are derived from resting macrophages that become primed by exposure to certain cytokines. Upon priming, these cells become positive for major histocompatibility (MHC) class II antigen and capable of functioning as antigen-presenting cells to T lymphocytes. Primed macrophages thus resemble dendritic cells. They can exit tissue sites by aﬀerent lymphatic vessels to reenter the lymph node. Activated macrophages are classically deﬁned as macrophages producing the full spectrum of inﬂammatory and cytotoxic cytokines; thus, they mediate and amplify acute inﬂammation, tumor killing, and major antibacterial activity. Epithelioid cells and giant cells represent diﬀerent terminal diﬀerentiations of the activated macrophage. Stimulated (or reparative) macrophages are partially activated and produce some inﬂammatory cytokines that contribute to ﬁbrosis and wound healing through the production of mitogens such as platelet- derived growth factors (PDGFs). They also contribute to angiogenesis through the production of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).

What test provides the most deﬁnitive evidence of sarcoidosis? The most appropriate next examination is gonioscopy. When a patient complains of monocular vision loss, it is imperative to know whether the visual loss truly involves 1 eye versus 1 homonymous ﬁeld of vision. With visual loss conﬁrmed in only 1 eye (as in this case, in which the patient covered the eyes alternately), vascular ﬂow or episodic inﬂammation/hyphema are considerations. Transient monocular vision loss of vascular origin is characterized by temporary loss of all sight in the eye (a blackout or whiteout ). However, this patient describes a cloudiness, which is more characteristic of a transient obscuring of the ocular media, especially considering the long duration of the vision loss and the slow recovery over 1-2 hours. In any patient who is pseudophakic and has symptoms suggestive of transient obscuring of the ocular media, uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome, in which chaﬁng of the iris by the optic/bag complex or the haptics causes transient intraocular bleeds, can be considered. In addition, the presence of phacodonesis on examination in this case makes UGH more likely. Gonioscopy is the key to the diagnosis of UGH syndrome, especially after the vision has cleared. A small layer of hemorrhage in the inferior angle provides evidence of the transient bleed. Automated visual ﬁelds would be beneﬁcial if a homonymous defect were suspected, as opposed to monocular loss of vision. Referral to cardiology for a Holter monitor and carotid Doppler images would be beneﬁcial if symptoms were suggestive of a transient monocular vision loss of vascular origin (ie, amaurosis fugax).

options.A: spiral or thin-cut computed tomography (CT) of the chest

explanation: Each of these diagnostic tests, if positive, support the diagnosis of sarcoidosis. The serum ACE level is moderately sensitive, but the lack of speciﬁcity limits the additive information that the ACE would provide when compared to a chest radiograph.

question: Chronic uveitis after cataract surgery, when it is attributed to the intraocular lens (IOL), is most commonly caused by what problem?

Chronic postoperative endophthalmitis, such as that associated with Propionibacterium acnes sequestered in the capsular bag, typically presents with chronic inﬂammation that persists beyond the initial postoperative period and should be considered on the diﬀerential diagnosis. question: The risk of what condition is thought to be minimized by the enucleation of NLP (no light perception) eyes within 14 days of penetrating injury?
explanation: Immune system sensitization to choroidal antigens is less likely if the inciting tissues are removed within 14 days of exposure. Therefore, some recommend enucleation of NLP (no light perception) eyes within 2 weeks following visually unrecoverable penetrating ocular injury to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia. Proliferative vitreoretinopathy may occur following penetrating injury, but its management with enucleation is not time-dependent. Similarly, bacterial endophthalmitis and/or phacoantigenic uveitis can be managed medically or by enucleation, and if surgical removal is necessary, it can be performed when required for medical management or cosmesis.

question: Band keratopathy is a common complication in what form of uveitis?

options.B: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)- associated anterior uveitis

explanation: Band keratopathy is a complication of chronic intraocular inﬂammation, typically more common when the predominant site of inﬂammation is the anterior segment. Of the choices provided, only JIA-associated anterior uveitis is a chronic uveitis. HLA-B27-associated uveitis and herpetic iridocyclitis are both acute, episodic forms of uveitis and typically do not result in band keratopathy (Note: inadequately treated forms of B27 acute anterior uveitis can take on a more "chronic" nature that can eventually produce band keratopathy, but this is not common). Toxoplasma-associated uveitis is predominantly a posterior uveitis that is also episodic in nature and does not typically result in band keratopathy. Aggressive inﬂammation associated with toxoplasmosis can produce anterior segment inﬂammation, as well, but the episodic nature of this type of inﬂammation precludes the chronic inﬂammation necessary to produce band keratopathy.

question: What immunosuppressive agent commonly used as a corticosteroid- sparing agent for ocular inﬂammatory disease is most likely to have gingival hyperplasia as an unwanted side eﬀect?
explanation: Gingival hyperplasia is one of the well-known side eﬀects speciﬁc to cyclosporine therapy. Cyclophosphamide is typically associated with leukopenia, hemorrhagic cystitis, sterility, and reversible alopecia. Azathioprine and methotrexate are both antimetabolites typically associated with gastrointestinal discomfort and hepatotoxicity.

question: What symptom(s) characterize(s) the presentation of serpiginous choroiditis?

options.A: sudden onset of central or paracentral scotoma
options.B: sudden profound complete loss of vision
options.C: gradual loss of vision with pain and photophobia

explanation: Serpiginous choroiditis, also termed geographic or helicoid choroidopathy, is likely inﬂammatory, but it typically does not manifest with signiﬁcant vitreous or anterior segment inﬂammation. Because of this, ﬂoaters and photophobia are not cardinal symptoms. The onset of symptoms is relatively sudden with a painless, unilateral, paracentral scotoma and potentially decreased vision, but it may proceed asymmetrically and with intermittent periods of progression. Many patients progress to vision of 20/200 or worse with involvement of the macula, but this decline in visual acuity typically develops over months or years. Patients may require aggressive anti-inﬂammatory treatment and need to be followed closely for the development of choroidal neovascularization and progression of disease. Tuberculosis-associated disease should be considered in the diﬀerential diagnosis.

question: What is the most common cause of decreased vision in patients with uveitis?
explanation: Uveitic macular edema is the most common cause of vision loss in eyes with uveitis. Uveitic glaucoma can develop from a combination of mechanisms, including from treatment with steroid medications. Choroidal neovascularization can develop in uveitis due to disruption of the Bruch membrane from choroidal inﬂammation and the presence of inﬂammatory cytokines that promote angiogenesis. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment occurs in 3% of patients with uveitis and is most commonly associated with panuveitis and infectious uveitis.

question: A 56-year-old woman presents for evaluation of right eye irritation. question: A patient presents with many episodes of recurrent nongranulomatous anterior uveitis. As part of the workup, the ophthalmologist orders puriﬁed protein derivative (PPD) placement and makes an appointment with the patient for 48 to 72 hours after the test to discuss the result. explanation: Delayed hypersensitivity (DH; previously termed Coombs and Gell type IV) represents the prototypical adaptive immune mechanism for lymphocyte-triggered inﬂammation. It is especially powerful in secondary immune responses. Previously primed DH CD4 T lymphocytes leave the lymph node, home into local tissues where antigen persists, and become activated by restimulation with the speciﬁc priming antigen and major histocompatibility (MHC) class II– expressing antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Fully activated DH T lymphocytes secrete mediators and cytokines, leading to the recruitment and activation of macrophages and/or other nonspeciﬁc leukocytes. The term delayed for this type of hypersensitivity refers to the fact that the reaction becomes maximal 12–48 hours after antigen exposure. The T helper-1 (Th1) subset of cytokines, especially interferon gamma (IFN-γ; also known as macrophage-activating factor) and tumor necrosis factor-beta (TNF-β), activates macrophages to secrete inﬂammatory mediators and kill pathogens, thus amplifying inﬂammation. Th1-mediated DH mechanisms, therefore, are thought to produce the classic DH reaction (eg, the puriﬁed protein derivative [PPD] skin reaction). +.

question: A 65-year-old man with an indwelling catheter presents with the gradual onset of a nongranulomatous uveitis with keratic precipitates, a hypopyon, and vitreous precipitates like a string of pearls in the right eye. explanation: Endogenous fungal endophthalmitis develops slowly as focal or multifocal areas of chorioretinitis. The infection usually begins in the choroid, appearing as yellow-white lesions with indistinct borders that range in size from small (cotton-wool spots) to several disc diameters. question: What time course characterizes recurrent uveitis as deﬁned by the Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) Working Group?

options.A: episodes of uveitis that recur more than 3 months after treatment has been discontinued
options.B: episodes of uveitis that resolve in fewer than 3 months
options.C: episodes of uveitis that recur irrespective of when treatment has been discontinued
options.D: episodes of uveitis that recur less than 3 months after treatment has been discontinued

explanation: Episodes of uveitis that recur less than 3 months after treatment has been discontinued are classiﬁed as chronic uveitis. Acute uveitis is deﬁned as resolving in fewer than 3 months. The answer choice “episodes of uveitis that recur irrespective of when treatment has been discontinued” is not a currently accepted classiﬁcation of uveitis. Recurrent uveitis is classiﬁed as disease in which patients exhibit periods of quiescence that last longer than 3 months, oﬀ of therapy.

question: What dosage of oral prednisone is considered to be the threshold for increasing toxicity that can induce osteoporosis?
explanation: The risk of osteoporosis is higher for postmenopausal women and men older than 50 years who take ≥7.5 mg/day of prednisone or its equivalent for longer than 3 months. To lessen the risk, patients receiving long-term corticosteroid maintenance therapy should supplement their diets with calcium and vitamin D, except with certain medications; the advice of the physician prescribing those drugs should be obtained.

question: What would be the preferred management of a 12-year-old child who demonstrates the ﬁndings shown?
explanation: This picture shows intraocular cysticercosis. Antihelminthic drugs can be helpful for neural cysticercosis, and a systemic evaluation is important, but antihelminthic drugs do not penetrate well into the eye. Laser can be helpful for small organisms under the retina, but larger and killed parasites can incite inﬂammation. The prognosis if untreated is poor, often with phthisis in 3–5 years. Surgical removal is the preferred treatment of this parasite. Antihelminthic medication (including albendazole) is useful for neurocysticercosis, but is not eﬀective for ocular infection.

question: A 62-year-old patient with history of multiple surgeries to the right eye for penetrating trauma presents with bilateral granulomatous panuveitis responding to high-dose oral corticosteroids. What is the most likely mechanism of his inﬂammation?

question: What infectious organism is mostly likely to cause chorioretinitis adjacent to a chorioretinal scar?
explanation: The most common cause of chorioretinitis is toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasmosis often recurs adjacent to scars indicating a prior episode, but it can also occur at "de novo" locations in the fundus. Acute retinal necrosis (usually secondary to herpes simplex virus or varicella zoster virus) and cytomegalovirus retinitis are not likely to be associated with pre-existing scars. Congenital rubella syndrome may cause diﬀuse retinal pigment epithelial mottling but is not classically associated with a pre-existing chorioretinal scar.

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with a 1-week history of right eye pain and photophobia. explanation: This patient has a positive CCP test result. In addition to the rheumatoid factor (RF) test, the CCP test is helpful in diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis. The sensitivity and speciﬁcity is increased when both RF and CCP show positive results, but in the setting of painful joints, rheumatoid arthritis is the most likely diagnosis.

question: According to the Systematic Nomenclature of Uveitis (SUN) system, what cell count per high powered ﬁeld (high-intensity slit beam at 45° to the visual axis, 1 mm × 1 mm) corresponds to a grade 1+ cell in the anterior chamber?

question: A 23-year-old man presents with sudden-onset eye pain and the eye appearance shown. He reports a previous history of similar symptoms in the contralateral eye. What systemic symptom is most likely to be present?
explanation: This ﬁgure demonstrates acute anterior uveitis with a hypopyon. The clinical features and the history of another episode in the fellow eye is strongly suggestive of HLA-B27-associated anterior uveitis. HLA-B27 is associated with a class of rheumatic diseases that have a predilection for the spinal and sacroiliac (axial) joints. The predominant symptom is low back pain. When the inﬂammation does not aﬀect the axial joints, HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies characteristically aﬀect the entheses (ligament or tendon attachment to bone). The heel and Achilles tendons are common targets. Other features include asymmetric oligoarthritis and inﬂammation of the ﬁngers and toes, resulting in "sausage digits." There are many spondyloarthropathies, including ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and enteropathic arthropathies linked to inﬂammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease).

question: What is the tissue-equivalent immune cell of the basophil?
explanation: Basophils are the blood-borne equivalent of the tissue-bound mast cell. Once basophils leave the bloodstream and take residence in tissue, they become mast cells. The other answer choices (macrophage, dendritic cell, Langerhans cell) are incorrect pairings of blood- and tissue-equivalent cells. Monocytes are the blood-borne equivalent of tissue-bound macrophages. Blood dendritic cells are precursors of tissue and lymphoid organ dendritic cells (they are not given a diﬀerent name). Eosinophils are not given a diﬀerent name in tissue.

question: At what level of the cornea are the deposits in the condition depicted (ﬁgure) primarily found?
explanation: Band keratopathy results from the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite at the level of the Bowman layer. Aside from chronic inﬂammation associated with uveitis, other causes of calciﬁc band keratopathy include systemic disorders that cause hypercalcemia or elevated serum phosphorus, as well as silicone oil (particularly in an aphakic eye), exposure to mercurial vapors or preservative, and primary hereditary band keratopathy. In ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) chelation to treat band keratopathy, the epithelium must be removed before the chelating solution is applied.

question: What antiparasitic therapy is most commonly used to slow the progression of onchocerciasis?
explanation: Ivermectin, given every 3 to 6 months, as long as there is evidence of skin or eye infection (along with a 6-week course of doxycycline), is the treatment of choice for onchocerciasis. Ivermectin safely kills the microﬁlariae, but it does not have a permanent eﬀect on the adult worms. Doxycycline targets Wolbachia, a parasitic bacterium that infects the adult worms and is crucial to their sexual development. Elimination of Wolbachia generally sterilizes and hastens the death of the worms.

question: What inhibitor of tumor necrosis factor α, useful for treating nonocular inﬂammation, is less eﬀective for uveitis?
explanation: Etanercept, a tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) decoy receptor, has proved eﬀective in controlling joint inﬂammation in polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) and adult rheumatoid arthritis. It is generally less eﬀective than inﬂiximab and adalimumab for uveitis and is not a preferred biologic for uveitis treatment. There are also some reports of paradoxical inﬂammation with etanercept. Golimumab is a TNF antagonist that is a monoclonal antibody similar to inﬂiximab and adalimumab, but data on its usefulness in uveitis are needed.

question: Progressive outer retinal necrosis may be distinguished from acute retinal necrosis by the presence of what feature?

explanation: The essential diﬀerence between progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN) and acute retinal necrosis (ARN) is the presence of an intact immune function in ARN. Both PORN and ARN are typically caused by herpes family viruses, speciﬁcally herpes simplex types 1 and 2, and the herpes zoster or varicella virus. Goldmann-Witmer coeﬃcient together with PCR increase the yield of diagnosing viral infections. The HLA-A29 genotype is associated with birdshot chorioretinopathy, and has not been reported in relation to viral retinitis. While HLA Aw33 phenotype has been reported to increase the relative risk of developing ARN in Japanese patients.

question: A myopic male patient with a history of lattice degeneration presents with mild distortion of the vision in the right eye for 2 weeks. explanation: This patient has all the risk factors for retinal detachment; he is myopic and has lattice degeneration. question: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)– associated uveitis occurs most commonly in oligoarticular-onset JIA, and a subset typically aﬀects girls who test positive for ANA. What should the treatment strategy include?

Because the long-term use of both oral and topical corticosteroids typically leads to signiﬁcant complications in children, it is important to consider systemic IMT early in the disease course.

question: What is the treatment for visually signiﬁcant calciﬁc band keratopathy?
explanation: Not all band keratopathy needs to be treated, but if it is symptomatic or visually signiﬁcant, the treatment is epithelial debridement followed by chelation with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA).

question: What phase of the immune response arc is constituted by the initial recognition, transport, and presentation of antigenic substances to the adaptive immune system?
explanation: Following ingestion of antigen, antigen-presenting cells (APCs) migrate via aﬀerent lymphatics to lymph nodes. In the APCs, enzymatic digestion of proteins within endocytic vesicles produces short amino acid chains of 7–11 amino acids: the antigenic epitopic fragments. Each antigenic fragment is combined with a groove-shaped HLA peptide residing on the APC surface, and this surface complex forms a unique epitope. question: What uveitic condition is characterized by the appearance of blood vessels in the anterior chamber angle without formation of peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS)?
explanation: Fuchs uveitis syndrome (sometimes called Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis [FHI] or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) is a chronic, mild, and typically unilateral uveitis associated with secondary open-angle glaucoma. Fine blood vessels are seen in the angle; they bridge the angle structures but do not grow or cause ﬁbrosis like rubeotic vessels. Posner-Schlossman syndrome, or glaucomatocyclitic crisis, is characterized by recurrent episodes of mild, unilateral iritis with marked elevation of intraocular pressure (IOP) into the 40-60 mm Hg range. With repeated episodes, secondary open-angle glaucoma may develop. As in Fuchs uveitis syndrome, PAS do not develop, but unlike in Fuchs uveitis syndrome, angle vessels are not seen in Posner- Schlossman syndrome. Synechiae are common in both VKH disease and juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

question: Where is the density of Langerhans cells highest in a healthy cornea?

options.D: not present in any portion of cornea

explanation: Langerhans cells (LCs) are important components of the immune system and play roles in antigen presentation, control of lymphoid cell traﬃc, diﬀerentiation of T lymphocytes, and induction of delayed hypersensitivity. In the conjunctiva and limbus, LCs are the only cells that constitutively express MHC class II molecules. LCs are present in the peripheral cornea, and any stimulation to the central cornea results in central migration of the peripheral LCs. There are typically no antigen-presenting cells found in either the central cornea or in the sclera in a healthy eye. LCs are typically found in vascularized areas, such as the conjunctiva and the limbus.

question: What ﬁnding is most likely in an eye with Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis (FHIC; also called Fuchs uveitis syndrome or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) in the absence of prior surgery?
explanation: Diﬀuse stellate keratoprecipitates are typically seen in FHIC and do not follow the pattern of the Arlt triangle, but are rather diﬀusely spread over the endothelial surface (similar to many other viral uveitides; there is data in the literature that now suggests FHIC is likely to be Rubella- associated anterior uveitis, which would place FHIC in the viral uveitides category). The diﬀuse stellate KP of FHIC are not symptomatic and should not be treated with corticosteroids, as not only do they not respond to treatment, but corticosteroids will only raise the risk of cataract formation and a steroid-induced pressure response. Patients with FHIC are not at risk for acute pressure spikes, but are at risk for the development of chronic, secondary open-angle glaucoma (along with cataracts and ﬂoaters) and should be followed as glaucoma suspects. Patients with FHIC typically do not present with CME, especially in the absence of prior surgery. While patients with FHIC can form posterior synechiae AFTER cataract surgery, the question speciﬁcally asks about the presence of posterior BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What treatment is likely to resolve human T-lymphotropic virus type -1 (HTLV-1) -associated retinal vasculitis?
explanation: Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is a retrovirus endemic to Japan, the Caribbean Islands, and Central and South America. About 1% of uveitis cases in Japan are due to HTLV-1. HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL), HTLV-1- associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paralysis (HAM/TSP), and HTLV-1 uveitis. Most cases of HTLV-1 uveitis (HU) are classiﬁed as intermediate uveitis (75%). Patients also present with keratopathy, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient with bilateral pars planitis who is being treated with mycophenolate mofetil exhibits recurrent uveitic macular edema (UME) in the right eye. What is the best initial choice in managing the macular edema in this patient? keratoconjunctivitis sicca, mild granulomatous uveitis, unilateral vitritis, membranous vitreous opacities, and snowballs. Retinal vasculitis, exudative retinal lesions, optic nerve abnormalities, and cystoid macular edema may be seen. HU is an inﬂammatory condition, probably due to inﬂammatory cytokines released by HTLV-1-infected CD4+ T cells, so retinal vasculitis is very responsive to systemic corticosteroids. Individuals infected with HTLV-1 are at risk for other opportunistic infections, as HTLV-1 alters the host immune response, so other infectious etiologies including HIV, syphilis, and cytomegalovirus (CMV) should be considered in HTLV-1 carriers. Zidovudine is used in human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV), (formerly termed HTLV III), infection. Intravitreal methotrexate is used for ocular involvement with primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma. It is not indicated in retinal vasculitis associated with HTLV-1.

explanation: Uveitic macular edema is a frequent complication of uveitis and may occur even when inﬂammation is otherwise controlled. Optical coherence tomography of the macula can help identify contributing factors to the macular edema, such as vitreomacular traction. If there is prominent vitreomacular traction, a pars plana vitrectomy may be considered. In this case, however, although there is uveitic macular edema, the imaging is otherwise unremarkable. If there were persistently active intraocular inﬂammation that may be driving the uveitic macular edema, advancing a patient’s systemic therapy may be beneﬁcial. However, this patient’s intraocular inﬂammation is inactive. In addition, advancing therapy from an antimetabolite (mycophenolate mofetil) to an alkylating agent (cyclophosphamide) is not indicated, because alkylating agents are reserved for aggressive, sight- threatening causes of ocular inﬂammation due to their signiﬁcant side eﬀects. Similarly, intravenous methylprednisolone would not be indicated as the ﬁrst step in managing this patient’s macular edema, although such therapy can be used initially for robust intraocular inﬂammation that must be managed quickly and requires doses higher BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

Onchocerciasis is one of the leading causes of blindness ( river blindness ) in Central America, South America, and sub-Saharan Africa. It is caused by the parasite Onchocerca volvulus and is transmitted by the black ﬂies of Simulium genus. The larvae develop into mature worms that migrate to the skin and form subcutaneous nodules. Any part of the eye, from the conjunctiva and cornea to the uvea and posterior segment, including the retina and optic nerve, may be involved. Microﬁlariae can even be observed swimming in the anterior chamber. The microﬁlariae migrate to the surface of the cornea, causing punctate keratitis, or sclerosing keratitis if the infection is chronic. Over time, the entire cornea may become opaque, thus leading to blindness. Mild to severe anterior uveitis, secondary glaucoma, and cataract may develop. Posterior segment ﬁndings may include early disruption of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), as well as pigment dispersion and atrophy. These may ensue in severe chorioretinal atrophy and optic atrophy. Behçet disease classically aﬀects young males who have a history of oral ulcers and have explosive inﬂammatory ocular response. HIV/AIDS retinopathy usually is characterized by microvascular changes, such as cotton-wool spots, microaneurysms, and telangiectasias, and later subsequently described with secondary opportunistic infections. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease presents as a panuveitis with a prodromal, uveitis, convalescent, and recurrent stage.

options.B: decreased aqueous production by ciliary body
options.D: anterior rotation of ciliary body due to shallow choroidal eﬀusions

explanation: Of the answer choices provided, resolution of inﬂammatory anterior choroidal eﬀusions in the setting of corticosteroid therapy will often result in posterior rotation of the ciliary body (CB) back to its native state, relieving the patient of secondary angle closure. (Another scenario where corticosteroid therapy in the setting of uveitis and elevated IOP can help lower the IOP is when there is an associated "trabeculitis," oftentimes seen in viral anterior uveitides). Of course, cycloplegics should also be used when anterior rotation of the ciliary body is thought to be a cause of increased IOP. Elevated IOP due to synechial angle closure will not respond to corticosteroid therapy, nor will a steroid response (in fact, it will only get worse with continued corticosteroids). Decreased aqueous production by the CB is one of the reasons patients with uveitis tend to have lower-than-baseline IOPs; treatment with corticosteroids causes resolution of intraocular inﬂammation and typically results in elevation of IOP back to baseline in these patients.

question: What is the most likely ﬁnding in a person who is HLA-A29 positive?

question: What type of macrophage expresses scavenging receptors but synthesizes very low levels of proinﬂammatory cytokines?
explanation: Resting macrophages are the classic scavenging cell, capable of phagocytosis and uptake of dead cell membranes, chemically modiﬁed extracellular protein (ie, acetylated or oxidized lipoproteins), sugar ligands, naked nucleic acids, and bacterial pathogens. Resting monocytes express at least 3 types of scavenging receptors but synthesize very low levels of proinﬂammatory cytokines. Scavenging can occur in the absence of inﬂammation. Primed macrophages are derived from resting macrophages that become primed by exposure to certain cytokines. Upon priming, these cells become positive for major histocompatibility (MHC) class II antigen and capable of functioning as antigen-presenting cells to T lymphocytes. Primed macrophages thus resemble dendritic cells. They can exit tissue sites by aﬀerent lymphatic vessels to reenter the lymph node. Activated macrophages are classically deﬁned as macrophages producing the full spectrum of inﬂammatory and cytotoxic cytokines; thus, they mediate and amplify acute inﬂammation, tumor killing, and major antibacterial activity. Epithelioid cells and giant cells represent diﬀerent terminal diﬀerentiations of the activated macrophage. question: What does the diﬀerential diagnosis of a 3-year-old child with hypopyon uveitis include?
explanation: Retinoblastoma is the most common malignant ocular tumor of childhood. In familial cases, it presents in the ﬁrst year of life or between ages 1 and 3 in sporadic unilateral cases. The most common initial sign is leukocoria, followed by strabismus, vitreous hemorrhage, hyphema, hypopyon, ocular/periocular inﬂammation, glaucoma, and proptosis. Occasionally, the malignant cells enter the anterior chamber and present as pseudohypopyon. Hypopyon in childhood is retinoblastoma, until proven otherwise. Retinal dysplasia, FEVR, Norrie disease, and Stickler syndrome do not present with hypopyon uveitis.

question: What is the ﬁrst-line treatment in patients with unilateral nodular anterior scleritis and no known systemic disease association?
explanation: Oral NSAIDs are ﬁrst-line therapy for nodular anterior scleritis, as long as infectious causes have been excluded and there are no contraindications to NSAID use. Topical corticosteroids will have minimal to no eﬀect in this setting, while oral corticosteroids and IMT are reserved for more severe cases and those refractory to oral NSAIDs.

question: An individual infected with the human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) has necrotizing retinitis. What test would be most helpful in making the diagnosis?

Intraocular antibody production can be computed using Goldmann-Witmer (GW) coeﬃcient. Polymerase chain reaction is the most sensitive, speciﬁc, and rapid mode of diagnosis for early initiation of appropriate therapy. Serum and urine testing for these agents may be contributory but not diagnostic of ocular infection.

question: A patient presents with bilateral snowballs and snowbanking. No retinal or choroidal lesions are seen. Results of an exhaustive systemic workup were negative. What ﬁndings would an ophthalmologist most likely see on ﬂuorescein angiography in the retinal periphery?
explanation: The major site of inﬂammation in intermediate uveitis is vitreous. "Snowballs" and "snowbanking" are common. Retinal phlebitis is a common occurrence and leads to the peripheral venous leakage seen on ﬂuorescein angiography. Anterior chamber cells can occur in adults (this is more common in children), but this reaction is very mild. Cystoid macular edema (CME) is a common cause of vision loss. Ischemia due to phlebitis and angiogenic stimuli from inﬂammation can result in neovascularization and vitreous hemorrhage, including retinal detachment. Dalen-Fuchs nodules are seen in sympathetic ophthalmia, Vogt- Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, and sarcoidosis.

question: What cell type produces antibodies?
explanation: Antibodies, or immunoglobulins, are produced by plasma cells derived from B lymphocytes after appropriate antigenic stimulation with T- lymphocyte help. Plasma cells initially secrete IgM antibodies, followed later by production of other isotypes after antibody-class switching. Antibodies are released into the eﬀerent lymph ﬂuid, draining into the venous circulation. Once bound to their speciﬁc epitope, antibodies mediate a variety of immune eﬀector activities, including opsonization for phagocytosis and complement activation via the classical pathway.

question: In a patient with anterior chamber and vitreous cells and macular edema, what information would best help support a diagnosis of retinitis pigmentosa (RP)?
explanation: Patients with RP often have variable numbers of vitreous and anterior chamber cells and can develop macular edema. Features of RP that diﬀerentiate it from uveitis include nyctalopia, positive family history, and, on fundus examination, waxy disc pallor, attenuation of arterioles, and a bone-spicule pattern of pigmentary changes in the mid- periphery. Electroretinographic (ERG) responses of patients with RP often appear severely depressed or extinguished. However, these ﬁndings can be seen in late posterior uveitis, making diﬀerentiation between the entities very diﬃcult in some cases.

question: What test is most appropriate in the initial workup of a patient with uveitis suspected of having sarcoidosis?
explanation: Chest x-ray is the single best screening modality for patients suspected of having sarcoidosis, as it reveals abnormalities in approximately 90% of patients who have sarcoidosis. The classic feature of a chest x-ray (CXR) in this setting is hilar lymphadenopathy, although chest computed tomography (CT) may also reveal mediastinal and other parenchymal abnormalities. Although retinal angiography may reveal leakage from retinal vasculitis (technically, retinal phlebitis), retinal vasculitis is not speciﬁc to sarcoidosis and can be seen in several other posterior uveitides. ANA and CRP have no screening value for patients suspected of having sarcoidosis. question: Within what ethnic group or geographic region is birdshot chorioretinopathy most prevalent?

There are several lens-induced glaucomas; 3 are secondary open- angle (phacoantigenic [previously termed phacoanaphylactic], phacolytic, lens-particle), and 1 is secondary angle-closure (phacomorphic). Phacoantigenic uveitis is a form of uveitis that develops when a patient is sensitized to his or her own lens protein. It often occurs in a posttraumatic setting, with disruption of the lens capsule. Since the immune sensitization does not involve immunoglobulin E (IgE), the stem anaphylaxis of the older term, phacoanaphylactic, is confusing. The presentation of phacoantigenic uveitis is of a granulomatous uveitis (ie, large, greasy or mutton-fat keratic precipitates, iris nodules). In this vignette, the mature cataract and keratic precipitates are suggestive of violation of the lens capsule and associated phacoantigenic uveitis. Phacolytic uveitis, also termed phacolytic glaucoma, is a complication of a mature or hypermature (liqueﬁed) cataract that results in the leaking of lens proteins through an intact lens capsule. Typical ﬁndings include cells, ﬂare, and lens-engorged macrophages settled in the inferior trabecular meshwork. In contrast to phacoantigenic/phacoanaphylactic uveitis, there are usually no keratic precipitates or synechiae present. Lens particle glaucoma results from fragments of cortical lens obstructing the trabecular meshwork. In phacomorphic glaucoma, an enlarging or intumescent cataract grows in the anterior-posterior dimension and thus pushes the iris forward, leading to angle closure.

explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; formerly, Wegener granulomatosis), is a multisystem autoimmune disorder characterized by the classic triad of necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis of the upper and lower respiratory tract, focal segmental glomerulonephritis, and necrotizing vasculitis of small arteries and veins. Involvement of the paranasal sinuses is the most characteristic clinical feature of this disorder, followed by pulmonary and renal disease. Ocular or orbital involvement is found in 15% of patients at presentation and in up to 50% of patients during the course of the disease. question: An ophthalmologist is consulted about a man who has polyarthritis, diarrhea, altered mentation, and blurry vision. The ocular examination is notable for bilateral panuveitis, retinal vasculitis, and pendular vergence motions concurrent with mastication. What is the preferred treatment for the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pendular vergence movements coinciding with mastication is descriptive of oculomasticatory myorhythmia, which is pathognomonic for Whipple disease. Whipple disease is a rare infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, and the gold standard for diagnosis is a duodenal biopsy with periodic acid–Schiﬀ (PAS) staining. There is central nervous system involvement in approximately 10% of cases of Whipple disease, although intraocular involvement is rare, at approximately 5% of cases. Other possible manifestations of uveitis associated with Whipple disease include multifocal chorioretinitis and vitritis. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred treatment for this infection, although ceftriaxone or tetracycline are possible alternative therapies.

question: Once the diagnosis of sympathetic ophthalmia is established, what is the preferred initial management?

explanation: In the rare instances when sympathetic ophthalmia does follow either injury or surgery, standard treatments such as corticosteroids almost always control the inﬂammation. Therefore, enucleation or evisceration of an injured eye to minimize risk of sympathetic ophthalmia should be undertaken only when the eye is painful, structurally disorganized, and has no light perception. Panretinal photocoagulation has no place in managing this form of uveitis. question: A patient is being treated for ﬁrst- time presentation of undiﬀerentiated granulomatous iridocyclitis. The patient responds very well to hourly topical corticosteroid, but in the past 3 months, the patient's intraocular inﬂammation has recurred every time the ophthalmologist has tried to taper the steroid below 4 times/day. The patient is beginning to develop a posterior subcapsular cataract, and her intraocular pressure is now 23 mm Hg on 1 glaucoma drop. What would be the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Continue the steroid taper slowly and reassure the patient that this type of inﬂammation "burns out" with time.
options.B: Increase topical corticosteroids and initiate therapy with an antimetabolite (eg, methotrexate).
options.C: Increase topical corticosteroids and initiate therapy with oral acetazolamide.
options.D: Schedule the patient for glaucoma valve placement.

explanation: Although her increasing intraocular pressure is a concern, there are other options available to help control her intraocular inﬂammation and pressure, while avoiding surgery. On the other hand, simply increasing her topical corticosteroid and starting oral acetazolamide will only serve to temporize the same issue: namely, the patient needs a steroid- sparing agent to keep her intraocular inﬂammation under control and spare her the side eﬀects of steroids. Tapering the steroid and providing reassurance is incorrect, given that the patient's inﬂammation has ﬂared up when the ophthalmologist has tried to taper the dosing below 4 times per day. The correct option here would be to increase the topical corticosteroids to get her inﬂammation back under control, start some form of immunomodulatory therapy (typically an antimetabolite to start with) to maintain control of her inﬂammation while tapering the steroid, and manage her intraocular pressure during this time.

question: What external structures of an otherwise healthy eye do not typically contain antigen- presenting cells?
explanation: There are no antigen-presenting cells found in either the central cornea or the sclera in a healthy eye. The paracentral cornea and central cornea are normally devoid of antigen-presenting cells and avascular. Various stimuli such as trauma, infection, or certain cytokines can recruit antigen-presenting cells. Plasma-derived proteins such as complement, IgM, and IgG are present in moderate concentrations in the peripheral cornea. Langerhans cells are typically found in vascularized areas, such as the conjunctiva and the limbus. Macrophages can also be found within the conjunctiva. Langerhans cells are a subset of dendritic cells that are present in most human epithelial cells. Their main function is acting as accessory immunoregulatory cells that process and present antigens to T lymphocytes through the MHC class II molecule. By presenting processed antigens, they activate and initiate a response from the lymphocytes.

question: What is a major risk factor for the development of primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) and primary intraocular lymphoma?

options.B: history of central nervous system irradiation

explanation: The most signiﬁcant risk factor for the development of primary intraocular lymphoma and primary CNS lymphomas is immunodeﬁciency. This includes HIV infection (which increases the risk from 50- to 500-fold), iatrogenic immune suppression, and aging (half of all cases occur after 60 years of age). The incidence of PCNSL appears to be increasing and is projected to occur in 1 of every 100,000 immunocompetent patients.

question: What systemic disease should be considered in a previously healthy adult patient from Mexico with uveitis, seizures, and calciﬁcations in the central nervous system (CNS) on computed tomography (CT) scan?
explanation: Cysticercosis is the most common ocular tapeworm infection caused by Taenia solium, which is endemic to Mexico, Central and South America, Eastern Europe, Africa, and India. The eye and CNS are commonly aﬀected. It may involve the eye and the adnexae. Subretinal space may harbor the parasite. These larvae may cause exudative retinal detachment, perforate the retina, and invade the vitreous cavity. Larvae can be seen undulating in the vitreous or subretinal space. Neurocysticercosis presents with seizures and, less commonly, headaches. In developing countries, this is one of the most common causes of seizures. Cysts located within the ventricles of the brain can block the outﬂow of cerebrospinal ﬂuid and present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure. question: Sympathetic ophthalmia can be diﬀerentiated from Vogt-Koyanagi- Harada (VKH) syndrome by what feature?
explanation: Aside from a history of penetrating ocular trauma, sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) and VKH-associated uveitis are essentially identical, as both can manifest meningeal signs (although meningeal signs typically present after ocular inﬂammation in SO, whereas they precede ocular inﬂammation in VKH), both are bilateral, both respond well to corticosteroids, and both represent an autoimmune response to tissue pigment. question: For what form of uveitis is aspiration and laboratory examination of a patient's intraocular ﬂuid most likely to lead to a speciﬁc diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: a patient with chronic unilateral anterior uveitis
options.B: a patient with retinitis and vitritis
options.C: a patient with chronic bilateral anterior uveitis
options.D: a 14-year-old patient with sudden- onset bilateral anterior uveitis and acute interstitial nephritis

explanation: There are many infectious etiologies of retinitis, and the clinical appearance is sometimes nonspeciﬁc. In immunosuppressed patients, such as those with HIV and AIDS, the diﬀerential is even more broad. Most patients with viral retinitis will have infection secondary to one of the herpes viruses, such as herpes simplex 1 or 2 (HSV-1 or -2) or varicella zoster virus (VZV). However, Candida, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Toxoplasma gondii must also be considered in the appropriate scenario. Diagnostic aspiration of intraocular ﬂuid with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing can clarify the diagnosis. Chronic bilateral anterior uveitis is unlikely to be infectious in origin, although CMV, HSV, tuberculosis, leprosy, or other rare infections should also be considered if the history or examination suggests one of these diseases. A chronic unilateral anterior uveitis is more likely to be infectious than a bilateral case, due to the more frequent inclusion of HSV in this category, but in general is unlikely to be infectious in origin, and therefore diagnostic aspiration of intraocular ﬂuid is infrequently indicated. In a patient with acute interstitial nephritis and bilateral anterior uveitis, the presumptive diagnosis is the tubulointerstitial nephritis uveitis (TINU) syndrome, which does not require intraocular ﬂuid for diagnosis. Syphilis, which is on the diﬀerential for all of the etiologies discussed, is diagnosed with treponemal serum antibodies, and does not require intraocular ﬂuid.

question: In a patient with multifocal choroiditis, what is the preferred management of chronic inﬂammation?

explanation: Multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis is an idiopathic inﬂammatory disorder of choroid, retina, and vitreous. It is more common in young, myopic women. It presents with photopsias, enlarged physiologic blind spot, and decreased vision. Because this is a chronic, recurrent inﬂammatory disease, immunomodulatory therapy with steroids or steroid-sparing agents is recommended. A viral etiology with herpes simplex and Epstein-Barr virus has been suggested but not veriﬁed; antiviral therapy is not used. Intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs are important adjuncts for the treatment of CNV. There is no role of cryotherapy.

question: For a patient with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), also known as juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA), what combination of laboratory ﬁndings would indicate the greatest risk of developing iritis?
explanation: The group of JRA (or JIA) patients with the greatest likelihood of developing uveitis are those with positive ANA and negative RF results. The group with the lowest likelihood of developing uveitis, and therefore a decreased frequency of screening required, are those with the presence of RF without ANA antibodies, such as in Still disease. ANCA are antibodies directed against cytoplasmic azurophilic granules of neutrophils and monocytes that are speciﬁc markers for a group of related systemic vasculitides, including GPA, MPA, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome), renal limited vasculitis, and pauci- immunoglomerulonephritis. HLA-B27 is a major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I antigen present in approximately 6.1% of the US general population. It is strongly associated with acute anterior uveitis, ankylosing spondylitis, and reactive arthritis syndrome.

question: What test commonly gives a false- positive result in patients with leptospirosis?
explanation: False positives with the puriﬁed protein derivative (PPD) can occur in a patient who has had a prior bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination, atypical mycobacterial infections, and bladder cancer. Interferon gamma release assays (IGRAs) are much less frequently associated with false positives compared to PPD in the setting of prior BCG vaccination. Urine histoplasmin antigen testing is carried out when there is suspicion for Histoplasma capsulatum infection. False positives are rare. question: What is a typical lesion size in multifocal choroiditis?
explanation: In multifocal choroiditis, the choroidal lesions range from approximately 50 μm to 200 μm in diameter and are more typically located in the posterior fundus, concentrated in the macula and/or forming peripheral linear streaks. Active lesions appear as yellowish- white choroidal inﬁltrates and may be associated with a neurosensory retinal detachment, vascular sheathing, disc edema, and cystoid macular edema. question: What sight-threatening complication of uveitis is related to ciliary body dysfunction?
explanation: Ciliary body inﬂammation causes aqueous hyposecretion and low intraocular pressure (hypotony). Hypotony due to chronic ocular inﬂammation may cause macular choroidal folds (hypotony maculopathy), serous choroidal detachment, and cataract. Macular edema is due to active intraocular inﬂammation and is mediated by cytokines such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and IL-6, which cause retinal vascular leakage and retinal pigment epithelial dysfunction. Band keratopathy develops in chronic uveitis and is due to calcium deposition along the epithelial and Bowman layers.

question: What treatment is most likely to halt the visual loss of diﬀuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN)?
explanation: DUSN is presumed to be caused by Ancylostoma caninum or Baylisascaris procyonis, depending on geographic location. Findings can include recurrent episodes of unilateral decrease in vision, with multifocal retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) changes and inﬂammation, among other ﬁndings. Laser photocoagulation of the nematode can kill and halt the disease. Additionally, antihelminthic therapy has typically involved thiabendazole or albendazole, which can immobilize the nematode and allow for direct laser photocoagulation or can empirically treat a nematode that cannot be visualized. Atovaquone is not an appropriate therapy for DUSN. Instead, this antiparasitic agent is typically used in the treatment of toxoplasmosis. Intravitreal bevacizumab, a monoclonal antibody directed against vasoendothelial growth factor (VEGF) can be useful in the treatment of choroidal neovascular membranes, but will not halt the worm in DUSN. Systemic corticosteroids can help with inﬂammation, but do not aﬀect the helminth.

Ocular presentations of sarcoidosis are chronic granulomatous iridocyclitis, nummular corneal inﬁltrates, band keratopathy, iris granulomas, vitritis, optic nerve granuloma, and periphlebitis. Necrotizing vasculitis is more consistent with granulomatosis, polyangiitis, and Behçet disease. Touton giant cells are seen in juvenile xanthogranuloma. question: What is an expected side eﬀect associated with a tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) inhibitor?
explanation: Because TNF-α inhibitors interfere with the TNF signaling pathway involved in mediating inﬂammation (which can be an important response in ﬁghting infection), the use of such medications can increase the patient's susceptibility to infection. Thus, tuberculosis is typically evaluated prior to starting an anti-TNF medication. Additionally, it is important to determine whether patients at risk for certain fungal infections live in an area where those infections are endemic.

question: In what stage of the disease does Lyme disease (LD)–associated intermediate uveitis occur most commonly?
explanation: The most common ocular manifestation of early stage 1 LD is follicular conjunctivitis. LD-associated uveitis occurs most commonly in stage 2 disease and less commonly in stage 3. It can manifest as anterior, intermediate, and posterior uveitis and as panuveitis; intermediate is the most common. Granulomatous anterior chamber reaction, severe vitritis, papillitis, retinal vasculitis, neuroretinitis, and choroiditis with exudative retinal detachment can also occur.

question: Methotrexate produces its anti- inﬂammatory eﬀect by what mechanism of action?
explanation: Methotrexate, a folic acid analogue and inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase, inhibits DNA replication, but its anti-inﬂammatory eﬀects result from extracellular release of adenosine.

question: What white dot syndrome can be mimicked by tuberculosis infection?
explanation: It is important to distinguish presumed immune-mediated serpiginous choroiditis from infectious entities that can simulate the disease. Although herpetic and syphilitic choroiditis can occasionally mimic serpiginous choroiditis, much more commonly, Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause inﬂammation in a similar pattern. Results of tuberculin skin testing and the interferon-gamma release assay are usually positive for tuberculosis, although the chest x-ray often appears normal. The disease usually responds to anti-tuberculosis treatment, and corticosteroids may also be needed to control inﬂammation. An infectious etiology has not been suggested for multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (although it may be preceded by viral prodrome), birdshot chorioretinopathy, or punctate inner choroiditis. age 65 years or greater.

question: Toxocariasis is seen most commonly in what age group? serpiginous choroiditis or geographic/helicoid choroidopathy A. 64 Correct Answer multiple evanescent white dot syndrome B.
explanation: Children and young adults are aﬀected disproportionately. Ocular toxocariasis (OT) is a zoonotic infection caused by Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati. Dogs and cats, the deﬁnitive hosts of the roundworm, pass unembryonated eggs via their feces into the environment (often into the soil). According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 30% of dogs younger than 6 months may deposit Toxocara eggs in their feces, and 25% of cats are infected with Toxocara cati. After 2–4 weeks, those eggs embryonate and become infectious. Transmission to humans occurs through ingestion of soil or contaminated food, or the fecal–oral route. Exposure to playgrounds, sandboxes, kittens, and puppies, as well as the pica eating disorder, are risk factors. Rarely, humans may acquire the infection from undercooked meat. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data from 2011–2014 suggested an overall seroprevalence in the United States of 5.1%. In children, an increased rate of antibody positivity correlated to lack of health insurance. The prevalence was recently estimated to be 1% of a large uveitic population treated at tertiary care centers in northern California.

question: What would anterior chamber paracentesis of a patient with phacolytic uveitis most likely reveal?
explanation: Phacolytic uveitis (or phacolytic glaucoma, as it is frequently called) occurs with hypermature cataracts. The lens proteins leak through the hypermature lens capsule and clog the trabecular meshwork, causing elevated intraocular pressure. There are refractile bodies in the anterior chamber (lipid-laden macrophages, which can be demonstrated with aqueous tap); usually keratic precipitates and posterior synechiae are not seen. Touton giant cells are seen in juvenile xanthogranuloma. Heinz bodies are spherical erythrocytes with denaturized hemoglobin granules bound to the internal surface of the cell membrane. They are observed with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and are seen in ghost cell glaucoma. "Owl eye" inclusions are seen in cytomegalovirus infections.

question: In addition to herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus, what member of the herpesvirus family is most likely to cause unilateral anterior uveitis?
explanation: Viral infections may cause either anterior or posterior uveitis. The most common viruses causing uveitis are cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes zoster, and herpes simplex. CMV is being increasingly recognized in Asian populations as a cause of a chronic, unilateral anterior uveitis associated with elevated intraocular pressure. Epstein-Barr virus is the viral agent commonly associated with infectious mononucleosis (IM). A mild, self-limiting follicular conjunctivitis, usually appearing early in the course of the disease, is most common with acquired IM. Less frequently reported anterior ocular manifestations of acquired IM include epithelial or stromal keratitis; episcleritis; and bilateral, granulomatous anterior uveitis. HHV 6 and 7 do not cause uveitis. They cause a febrile illness in children called roseola that is characterized by high temperatures, followed by a rash that does not desquamate.

question: What is the most common form of ocular involvement in patients with ocular sarcoidosis?

Vitreous involvement is common and often presents as clumps of snowballs with or without diﬀuse cellular inﬁltration. question: What nonocular clinical feature is most common in patients with ocular Behçet disease (BD)?

Vasculitis and thrombophlebitis are less common. In some populations there is an association with HLA-B51, but this association lacks adequate predictive value for clinical use.

question: What factor is associated with vision loss in patients with ocular sarcoidosis?

question: What should be the ﬁrst mode of therapy in sarcoid-associated retinal and optic disc neovascularization?

options.B: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injection

question: Regional immunity can aﬀect what phase of the immune response arc?
explanation: The concept that many organs and tissue sites possess modiﬁcations to the classic immune response arc is called regional immunity. Regional immunity can aﬀect all 3 phases of the response arc—aﬀerent, processing, and eﬀector. Regional diﬀerences in immune response occur because of diﬀerences in the immunologic microenvironments of various tissue sites.

question: What diagnosis is demonstrated by the histopathology image shown?
explanation: Phacoantigenic uveitis develops when an amount of lens cortex is retained in an eye following cataract extraction or following traumatic lens capsule disruption. Histopathology (see ﬁgure with caption) will show zonal granulomatous inﬂammation at the site of lenticular trauma. The inﬂammation can be either granulomatous or nongranulomatous, with corresponding keratic precipitates. Phacolytic uveitis occurs when a hypermature cataract develops and high-molecular-weight lens proteins leak through the capsular bag into the anterior chamber. Macrophages ingest the lens proteins and become lipid laden, having a refractile appearance. Keratic precipitates in phacolytic uveitis are not typically seen. The treatment for both types of uveitis is typically surgical: Removal of the lens material will often cause resolution of the uveitis. If a very small amount of cortex is left in the anterior chamber in the case of phacoantigenic uveitis, topical corticosteroids are sometimes employed to manage modest inﬂammation until the lens material is resorbed by macrophages. Infectious endophthalmitis is a clinical diagnosis, and an aqueous or vitreous specimen may grow the infectious agent. question: An Asian patient presents with a recent history of bilateral uveitis with hearing disturbance complaining of poor vision. She has been told nothing can be done to improve her vision and comes for a second opinion. There are yellow- white subretinal scars in her fundus. explanation: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome occurs most commonly in people with Asian, Asian Indian, Hispanic, Native American, and Middle Eastern ancestry. There are 4 stages: prodromal, acute uveitic, convalescent, and chronic recurrent. This patient likely described having the prodromal and acute uveitic phases in her past. The prodromal stage is marked by ﬂulike symptoms. Auditory problems are observed in 75% of patients and frequently coincide with the onset of ocular disease. Central dysacusia, generally involving higher frequencies or tinnitus, aﬀects 30% of patients early in the disease course, typically improving within 2-3 months; however, persistent deﬁcits may remain. The acute uveitic stage is characterized by sequential blurring of vision in both eyes, 1-2 days after the onset of neurological symptoms, with bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis, varying degrees of vitritis, thickening of the posterior choroid, optic nerve edema and multiple serous retinal detachments. Several weeks later, the exudative retinal detachments resolve and gradual depigmentation of the choroid occurs, leading to the classic sunset-glow fundus. Integumentary changes (perilimbal vitiligo [Sugiura sign], vitiligo, alopecia, poliosis) occur during the convalescent stage. The chronic recurrent stage is characterized by recurrent bouts of granulomatous anterior uveitis, which may occur concomitantly with subclinical choroidal inﬂammation requiring systemic therapy. Visually debilitating sequelae of chronic inﬂammation develop during this last stage; they include posterior subcapsular cataract, glaucoma, CNV, and subretinal ﬁbrosis. The fundus exam in this patient most likely revealed subretinal ﬁbrosis. These changes have not been described in sympathetic ophthalmia. Susac syndrome is associated with hearing loss but does not have the retinal ﬁndings described. Instead, fundus exam reveals diﬀuse or localized narrowing of retinal arteries with a “boxcar” segmentation. Subretinal ﬁbrosis and uveitis is an uncommon panuveitis syndrome of unknown etiology with bilateral white-yellow lesions in the posterior pole that either fade without retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) alterations, become atrophic, or enlarge and coalesce into large, white, stellate zones of subretinal ﬁbrosis. It is not associated with auditory disturbances. The ﬁgures show various ﬁndings associated with diﬀerent phases of VKH. Note also, the diagnosis of VKH requires bilateral involvement and the absence of penetrating ocular injury and other ocular or systemic disease. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis initially. Topical and systemic steroids are the ﬁrst line of therapy, with immunosuppressants for recurrent or resistant cases. question: What is the etiology of multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis?
explanation: Multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis (MCP) is a condition characterized by intraocular inﬂammation and multifocal choroidal lesions occurring in the absence of a known ocular or systemic disease. The disease is typically bilateral and has a predilection for females in the second to sixth decades of life. The herpes simplex and Epstein- Barr viruses have been implicated in this disease process; however, a viral etiology has not been proven. Pathologic specimens obtained from eyes with MCP have shown variable ﬁndings, ranging from large numbers of B lymphocytes in the choroid to a predominance of T lymphocytes, suggesting that diﬀerent immune mechanisms may produce a similar clinical picture, and that an initial viral infection may trigger an autoimmune process. Treponema pallidum, Toxoplasma gondii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis are organisms that can be associated with posterior uveitis, but are not the etiology of MCP.

question: By what mechanism does cyclosporine treat uveitis?

options.A: inhibits T-cell receptor signal transduction and downregulates interleukin-2 (IL-2) activity

explanation: Types of immunomodulatory therapy (IMT), also known as immunosuppressive or disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), are often divided into nonbiologic-IMT and biologic agents. Cyclosporine is a nonbiologic-IMT, and furthermore is a T-cell T-cell inhibitor inhibitor, which is so-called due to its mechanism of action. Cyclosporine inhibits T-cells by inhibiting calcineurin, which then stops T-cell receptor signal transduction (T-cell signaling), and downregulates interleukin-2 (IL-2) activity. IL-2 is downregulated due to decreased IL- 2 gene transcription and receptor expression of CD4+ lymphocytes. Tacrolimus is the other T-cell inhibitor T-cell inhibitor or calcineurin inhibitor calcineurin inhibitor that is used for uveitis treatment. The other answers describe mechanisms of action (MOA) of other non- biologic and biologic IMT medications. Beside T-cell inhibitors T-cell inhibitors, nonbiologic-IMT medications also include antimetabolites antimetabolites and alkylating agents alkylating agents. Biologic agents are genetically engineered proteins targeting speciﬁc immune processes, and they include tumor tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) inhibitors necrosis factor α (TNF-α) inhibitors and inhibitors of others inhibitors of others proinﬂammatory mediators proinﬂammatory mediators. The answer choice "inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and DNA replication, and causes extracellular release of adenosine" describes the MOA of methotrexate, which is an antimetabolite antimetabolite. It is a folic acid analogue and dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor. It reduces DNA replication, but the anti-inﬂammatory mechanism occurs due to extracellular release of adenosine. The other antimetabolites used to treat uveitis include azathioprine, which is a purine nucleoside analogue that interferes with DNA replication and RNA transcription, and mycophenolate mofetil, which inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and DNA replication. The answer choice "alkylates purines in DNA and RNA causing abnormal DNA replication and cell death" describes the MOA of cyclophosphamide, which is an alkylating agent alkylating agent. It alkylates purines in DNA and RNA, causing impaired DNA replication and cell death. The other alkylating agent used to treat uveitis is chlorambucil, which also interferes with DNA replication. Cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil are typically reserved for severe, vision-threatening, or life-threatening inﬂammation that other less toxic therapies failed to manage. The answer choice "directly inhibits tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) as a fully human monoclonal immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) antibody against TNF-α" describes the MOA of the biologic agent adalimumab, which is a TNF-α inhibitor TNF-α inhibitor. It is a fully human monoclonal immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) antibody that targets TNF-α. It was the ﬁrst FDA-approved systemic medication for noninfectious uveitis. The other TNF-α inhibitor that is used for uveitis treatment currently is inﬂiximab. It is a mouse/human chimeric immunoglobulin G1 kappa (KgG1κ) monoclonal antibody against TNF-α. Within the category of biologic agents, besides TNF-α inhibitors, there are also others including rituximab, which is a chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20+ cells (mostly B lymphocytes), interferon alpha-2a/2b (IFN-α2a/2b), which has antiviral, immunomodulatory, and antiangiogenic eﬀects, and abatacept, which inhibits T-cell costimulation.

question: What is the resident macrophage of the retina?
explanation: Tissue-resident macrophages are monocytes that migrated into the tissue during embryologic development and later acquired tissue- speciﬁc properties and cellular markers. These resident macrophages are Kupﬀer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages in the lung, and microglia in the brain. Bipolar cells exist between photoreceptors (rod cells and cone cells) and ganglion cells. They act, directly or indirectly, to transmit signals from the photoreceptors to the ganglion cells. Amacrine cells are inhibitory neurons, and project their dendritic arbors to the inner plexiform layer (IPL), thereby interacting with retinal ganglion cells and/or bipolar cells. Horizontal cells are the laterally interconnecting neurons having cell bodies in the inner nuclear layer of the retina of vertebrate eyes. Horizontal cells provide inhibitory feedback to rod and cone photoreceptors.

The Coombs and Gell system of classifying adaptive immune-triggered inﬂammatory responses had 4 main categories of hypersensitivity: anaphylaxis, antibody-dependent cytotoxicity, immune complex reactions, and cell-mediated reactions, but this classiﬁcation predated the discovery of T lymphocytes. It is more accurate to divide the eﬀector responses into 3 main categories: antibody-mediated, lymphocyte mediated (delayed hypersensitivity and cytotoxic lymphocytes), and combined antibody and cellular mechanisms. Antibody-mediated responses utilize the 5 major classes of immunoglobulins (M,G,A,D and E) and subtypes. Allergic conjunctivitis triggered by IgE activation is an example. Lymphocyte-mediated delayed hypersensitivity occurs when previously primed DH CD4+ lymphocytes enter local tissue and react with antigens, becoming activated to secrete mediators and cytokines. The pattern of inﬂammatory response is included by the subtype of CD4+ T cell involved in the reaction. Some examples of lymphocyte- mediated delayed hypersensitivity include giant papillary conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis, sympathetic ophthalmia, and giant cell arteritis. Lymphocyte-mediated cytotoxic lymphocytes are a subset of T lymphocytes that usually exhibit the CD8 marker and are eﬀective at destroying tumor cells and virus-infected cells. Graft rejection utilizes this type of eﬀector response. A combined antibody and cellular mechanism is utilized if the antibody involved does not directly activate complement, but rather the antibody attracts leukocytes to attack the cell instead.

question: What infectious uveitic disorder may closely mimic acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)?
explanation: The placoid lesions in APMPPE occur at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and underlying choroid. Similar lesions can be a presentation in syphilitic chorioretinitis, and checking rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and ﬂuorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA- ABS) is an important part of the diagnostic evaluation of APMPPE (see Table). West Nile virus will appear as discrete punctate chorioretinal lesions that follow the retinal nerve ﬁber layer in a linear fashion. Herpetic uveitis can be varied in its presentation, from a granulomatous anterior uveitis to posterior retinitis, depending on whether HSV or VZV is the etiology. Acute retinal necrosis (ARN) can occur with either of these pathogens and may present as a panuveitis or a viral retinitis, even leading to retinal detachments. Toxoplasma gondii uveitis can present with many diﬀerent ﬁndings as well, depending on whether it is congenital or acquired. Acquired disease classically presents with a focal white retinochoroiditis with overlying vitreous inﬂammation ("headlight in the fog"), often adjacent to a chorioretinal scar.
