question: A 62-year-old patient presents with uveitis that has not responded to prolonged steroid therapy. He has vitreous haze without a clear view of the fundus. What is the next best step to obtain a diagnosis?

explanation: The presence of vitreous cells in cases of uveitis not responding to therapy necessitates a vitreous biopsy. An MRI of the brain is indicated to determine central nervous system (CNS) involvement, even in suspected primary intraocular lymphoma, regardless of the presence or absence of neurologic symptoms, but a vitreous specimen should be obtained as a primary step. HLA testing would not be indicated as an initial step in workup, and a ﬂuorescein angiogram is unlikely to provide useful information in conﬁrming a diagnosis of primary CNS lymphoma.

question: A 26-year-old man develops a high fever, arthralgias, skin rash, and decreased vision approximately 1 week after returning from a trip to India. On examination, he has bilateral diﬀuse pigmented keratic precipitates (KPs), elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), and conﬂuent areas of yellow-white changes with hemorrhages in the macula and along the arcades, with minimal vitritis. What viral disease is the most likely cause of these ﬁndings?
explanation: Chikungunya fever is caused by Alphavirus, typically transmitted to humans via mosquito bites. Maternal-fetal transmission has been documented as well. Outbreaks have occurred in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas, with a notable large outbreak in India in . There have been over 1.9 million cases since 2005 in India, Indonesia, Maldives, Myanmar, and Thailand. The patient's returning from India recently is 1 clue that he may have this virus. The incubation period is 2- 7 days, and causes systemic symptoms that include fever, fatigue, headache, nausea, vomiting, arthralgia, myalgia, and skin rash, similar to those of dengue fever. The ocular manifestations include both anterior uveitis and retinochoroiditis, and sometimes nodular episcleritis. Patients tend to have diﬀuse granulomatous or nongranulomatous pigmented pigmented KPs, iris iris pigment release pigment release, elevated elevated IOP, along with posterior pole focal, multifocal, or conﬂuent retinochoroiditis, retinal hemorrhages, and trace trace vitritis. This patient had pigmented KPs and elevated IOP with yellow-white changes in the macula and vascular arcades (posterior pole) suggestive of retinitis or retinochoroiditis, with minimal vitritis. The pigment may diﬀerentiate the anterior uveitis from other infectious etiologies, and very few uveitic processes cause elevated IOP, with herpetic uveitis being another. The absence of peripheral retinitis and signiﬁcant vitritis also diﬀerentiates it from other uveitides that aﬀect both anterior and posterior segments. Serologic testing for IgM antibodies, or virus isolation, or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing can conﬁrm the diagnosis. Systemic acyclovir and prednisone have been used to treat the retinitis; however, no evidence suggests that these improve visual outcomes. While CMV can also present with these ﬁndings (ie, CMV, like all viral anterior uveitis, can present with diﬀuse KP and elevated IOP, and CMV retinitis is very similar to the description in question stem), there is nothing to suggest the patient is immunocompromised (ie, CD4 < 50). Dengue fever has very similar systemic symptoms to those of chikungunya fever, and it is also transmitted by mosquitos and is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. However, beside fever, headache, and myalgia, there is a purpuric rash and there are more bleeding manifestations, due to thrombocytopenia. The most frequent ocular ﬁnding is petechial subconjunctival hemorrhage. Anterior chamber and vitreous cells can occur to a variable degree, but pigment release is not characteristic. Maculopathy or "foveolitis" is seen in around 10% of patients 1 month after systemic disease onset, and while no lesions are visualized on clinical examination, optical coherence tomography (OCT) may show macular edema, subretinal ﬂuid, or inner segment/outer segment junction disruption. Rift Valley fever is caused by the Bunyaviridae family and also causes fever, with 3 clinical presentations including ﬁrst, a febrile, inﬂuenza-like illness; second, a hemorrhagic fever; and third, encephalitis. It occurs mostly in sub-Saharan Africa, with an outbreak in Saudi Arabia, thus the patient's coming from India would make this choice less likely. Like chikungunya fever, it presents with anterior uveitis, and macular or paramacular retinitis, and retinal hemorrhages; however, this is also associated with mild to moderate vitritis, vasculitis, and optic nerve edema. Pigmented KPs and KPs in general are not characteristic of Rift Valley fever.

question: What is the ﬁrst step in the delayed hypersensitivity reaction that occurs in a positive puriﬁed protein derivative (PPD) test?

options.A: T lymphocytes primed in the hilar nodes circulating to the dermis
options.B: cytokines within the dermis inducing ﬁltration of lymphocytes, monocytes and ﬁbrin clotting
options.D: dermal macrophages ingesting the puriﬁed protein derivative (PPD) reagent

explanation: Following exposure to live tuberculin organisms in the lungs, alveolar macrophages ingest the microorganisms and travel to the hilar lymph nodes. B and T lymphocytes are primed and then recirculate to the lungs. Once the T lymphocytes encounter macrophage-ingested TB, cytokines are released that induce neighboring macrophages to diﬀerentiate into epithelioid cells and become caseating granulomas. A secondary skin response to injection of puriﬁed protein derivative (PPD) begins with dermal macrophages ingesting the antigen. These PPD-stimulated macrophages migrate into an adjacent lymph node, where they encounter memory T lymphocytes. The memory T lymphocytes then recirculate into the dermis, where they encounter other stimulated macrophages at the injection site. This fully activates the memory T lymphocytes to release cytokines locally. These cytokines induce inﬁltration of additional T lymphocytes, monocytes, and ﬁbrin clotting forming the indurated dermal lesion. Because this occurs in approximated 24 hours, it is called a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Type I hypersensitivity is triggered by the activation of IgE. The Fc portion of the IgE antibody binds to mast cells, causing them to degranulate and release interleukins and cytokines. This happens within several minutes of re-exposure. These inﬂammatory mediators can cause blood vessel dilation and massive edema, leading to reactions ranging from hives and urticaria to laryngeal edema and anaphylaxis. Type II hypersensitivity is deﬁned as a hypersensitivity reaction secondary to antibodies that are directly cytotoxic against human tissues. Examples of Type II hypersensitivity include Goodpasture syndrome and cicatricial pemphigoid. Type III hypersensitivity is deﬁned as a hypersensitivity secondary to antibody- antigen immune complex reactions. Examples of Type III hypersensitivity include systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis.

The ﬂuocinolone implant is unnecessary in this case because she is already being treated systemically, her disease is well controlled, and there is no macular edema. question: A middle-aged woman presents with photopsias in her right eye and circular white lesions on her fundus examination. Her ﬂuorescein angiogram (FA) and indocyanine green (ICG) image are shown in Figure 1. What management is recommended?
explanation: Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) is an uncommon idiopathic inﬂammatory condition of the retina. It usually aﬀects young, healthy, myopic females and presents with acute unilateral decreased vision, central or paracentral scotomata, and photopsias. Fluorescein angiography shows multiple punctate hyperﬂuorescent lesions in a wreath-like conﬁguration surrounding the fovea. ICG shows multiple, hypocyanescent lesions. Usually MEWDS is self-limited, and recovery is expected within 2-10 weeks without treatment. Systemic and intravitreal steroids are used to treat many other types of noninfectious uveitis. Intravitreal methotrexate has been used to treat both noninfectious uveitis and vitreoretinal lymphoma.

question: A 28-year-old woman presents with a history of photopsia of several months' duration. On examination there are no anterior chamber cells, keratic precipitates, or posterior synechiae. On examination after dilation, there is no vitritis, but there are several discrete lesions 100 μm to 200 μm diameter in the posterior segment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The patient described ﬁts the typical patient with PIC: a young woman (18-40 years old) with photopsias. Other visual symptoms include paracentral scotomas and metamorphopsia. In multifocal choroiditis (MC), the lesions may range from 50 μm to 200 μm in size (and thus can be similar in size to PIC lesions), but there is an accompanying vitritis as often as anterior chamber cell. Additionally, the lesions in PIC typically do not extend out to the midperiphery, whereas in MC they can also be found peripherally. The creamy yellow/whitish lesions in birdshot range from 50 μm to 1500 μm in size and lie at the level of the choroid. Patients with birdshot are typically middle-aged women (30-70 years of age). While this patient is of the appropriate gender for subretinal ﬁbrosis and uveitis syndrome (nearly all patients are young women), the lesions, which occur at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium, are larger than those described by this patient, and the inﬂammation is also characterized by inﬂammation in the anterior chamber and vitreous.

question: What type of necrotizing scleritis presents with progressive plaques of nonperfusion of the episclera and conjunctiva, adjacent to areas of severe congestion of the episclera, with scleral edema and inﬁltration usually sparing the limbus?
explanation: Necrotizing scleritis with inﬂammation is characterized by overt signs and symptoms of scleral inﬂammation. It may be subdivided into 3 types: (1) vaso-occlusive, (2) granulomatous, and (3) postsurgical. The vaso-occlusive type progressively displays plaques of nonperfusion of episclera/conjunctiva, associated with scleral edema/inﬁltration and severe congestion of adjacent episcleral/conjunctival vessels. The limbal area and peripheral cornea are often spared. These cases are usually associated with infection or with an underlying systemic immune-mediated disease. The granulomatous type typically starts with necrotizing inﬂammation of the limbal area, further extending anteriorly to the cornea and posteriorly to the sclera. The inﬂamed area assumes a “lumpy” aspect, associated with inﬂammatory inﬁltration and edema. question: What organism causes ocular toxocariasis?

A 29-year-old woman presents for evaluation of bilateral central vision loss and photopsias. She reports onset of fever, chills, headache, and malaise approximately 1 week ago. The ophthalmologist notes the fundus ﬁndings shown in the image, as well as corresponding early hypoﬂuorescence and late- phase staining. What life- threatening complication is associated with the most likely diagnosis in this scenario? Ocular toxocariasis (also termed ocular larval migrans) is a rare condition resulting from tissue invasion by the second-stage larvae of Toxocara canis or cati. Ocular larval migrans, with sparing of the viscera, often occurs in older children. In contrast, visceral larval migrans typically occurs in younger children. Toxoplasma gondii causes toxoplasmosis, which is a much more common retinochoroiditis and may be acquired or congenital. The Brucella species may cause a systemic infection in humans after exposure to infected animals, typically via ingestion of unpasteurized milk or cheese products. Onchocerciasis, caused by the ﬁlarial parasite Onchocerca volvulus, is one of the leading causes of blindness in sub-Saharan Africa. The ﬂies that carry the parasite breed in fast-ﬂowing streams, giving the disease its common name, river blindness.

Approximately half of aﬀected patients have a preceding viral prodrome, and men and women are aﬀected equally. Symptoms are typically bilateral, with fellow eye involvement occurring within a period of days to weeks. Typical fundus ﬁndings include large (1-2 disc diameters), yellow-white, placoid lesions distributed throughout the posterior pole to the equator. Fundus angiography typically demonstrates early hypoﬂuorescence corresponding to the lesions but often exceeding the areas visible funduscopically. In late phases, these lesions demonstrate late hypoﬂuorescent staining. These lesions typically involute over a period of several weeks, leaving behind signiﬁcant retinal pigment epithelial alteration.

question: In what stage are the majority of macrophages present in phacolytic glaucoma?

Why might a patient with acute leptospirosis have resolution of systemic symptoms but continuing uveitis? Macrophages exist in diﬀerent levels or stages of metabolic and functional activity, each representing diﬀerent programs of gene activation and synthesis of macrophage-derived cytokines and mediators. The categories of macrophages include: resting (immature or quiescent) primed activated stimulated or reparative Phagocytosis removes host cell debris in the process called scavenging. Resting macrophages are the classic scavenging cell, capable of phagocytosis and uptake of the following: dead cell membranes chemically modiﬁed extracellular protein (ie, acetylated or oxidized lipoproteins) such as lens protein released with damage to the lens capsule sugar ligands, through mannose receptors naked nucleic acids bacterial pathogens Resting monocytes express at least 3 types of scavenging receptors but synthesize very low levels of proinﬂammatory cytokines. Scavenging can occur in the absence of inﬂammation. Mild inﬁltration of scavenging macrophages centered around retained lens cortex or nucleus fragments occurs in nearly all eyes with lens injury. Phacolytic glaucoma is a variant of scavenging macrophage inﬁltration in which leakage of lens protein occurs through the intact capsule of a hypermature cataract. Lens protein–engorged scavenging macrophages present in the anterior chamber block the trabecular meshwork outﬂow channels, resulting in elevated intraocular pressure. Other signs of typical lens-associated uveitis are conspicuously absent. Experimental studies suggest that lens proteins may be chemotactic stimuli for monocytes.

options.C: Residual antigens from the acute ocular infection trigger molecular mimicry, resulting in sterile inﬂammation.

explanation: Leptospirosis is caused by a spirochetal bacterium commonly found in sewer water and rats. The majority of US cases occur in Hawaii. Because of its phylogenic similarity to other spirochetal bacteria such as Treponema pallidum, patients often have false-positive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) or ﬂuorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA- ABS) test results. If the systemic symptoms resolve but uveitis continues or recurs, persistence of leptospirosis in the eye, a privileged site, is the most likely cause. A unique feature of the microenvironment of the eye is termed the ocular immune privilege. The term was introduced in 1940s by the ﬁnding that foreign antigen introduction to the anterior chamber did not elicit inﬂammatory response. Immune privilege is thought to be an evolutionary adaptation to protect vital structures. Traditionally, central nervous system, eyes, and testicles are considered immune-privileged organs.

question: A patient complains of eye pain and blurry vision. The B-scan is shown. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: B-scan ultrasonography is the best diagnostic evaluation for identifying posterior scleritis. It can identify the classic "T-sign" (as shown by the arrow in the photo), which is localized posterior scleral thickening perpendicular to the optic nerve and forms a T-shaped shadow. Additionally, B-scan can identify areas of scleral thickening in other regions away from the optic nerve. Serpiginous choroiditis should have a normal B-scan. Choroidal eﬀusions have a diﬀerent appearance on B-scan, with dome- shaped retinal elevations with echolucent (dark) subretinal ﬂuid. Diﬀuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis may show changes in the optic nerve on B-scan, but it should not have a T-sign.

question: What complication of serpiginous choroiditis is suggested by the presence of subretinal ﬂuid and hemorrhage? Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium intracellulare B.
explanation: Subretinal ﬂuid and hemorrhage in a patient with serpiginous choroiditis is highly suspicious for choroidal neovascularization, a common and severe complication of this choroiditis. Active choroiditis can present with retinal whitening or be associated with decreased visual acuity, but does not typically present with hemorrhage. Choroidal rupture may mimic choroidal neovascularization and present with subretinal ﬂuid and hemorrhage. However, a supportive history or associated traumatic event would be expected. This would be uncommon in the elderly age group typically carrying the diagnosis of serpiginous choroiditis. Cystoid macular edema is rare with serpiginous choroiditis and would not present with subretinal ﬂuid and hemorrhage.

question: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with dense anterior and posterior uveitis and seizures. He had been to India during the past few months. A cranial computed tomography (CT) scan shows a very small calciﬁcation and hydrocephalus. A B-scan shows a centrally echo- dense, curvilinear, highly reﬂective structure superior to the optic nerve. What is the cause of the patient's illness?
explanation: The B scan structure showing a centrally echo-dense, curvilinear, highly reﬂective structure superior to the optic nerve is suggestive of the scolex and is characteristic of cysticercosis. Although the eye is more commonly aﬀected than any other organ, neural cysticercosis is associated with signiﬁcant morbidity and a mortality of 40%. Epileptiform seizures may be the ﬁrst sign of cerebral cysticercosis. Both anterior chamber and vitreous may demonstrate inﬂammatory activity; vitreous inﬂammation is more pronounced during the early stages of the disease.

question: A 25-year-old man who admits to intravenous (IV) drug use has a lesion on the left upper and lower lid (Figure 1). What additional diagnostic testing is most important for this patient?
explanation: The mass depicted is a Kaposi sarcoma. It presents as a reddish dermal mass and is a frequent manifestation of AIDS. These lesions are associated with human herpesvirus 8. In addition to the eyelid manifestations, conjunctival lesions can also present and appear similar to foreign body granulomas or cavernous hemangiomas. Histologically, they are composed of spindle cells. Treatment can include cryotherapy, excision, radiation, or intralesional chemotherapeutic agents. Often, these lesions can regress following immune reconstitution with adequate antiviral treatment of the HIV infection.

question: In the setting of anterior uveitis, what ﬁnding is most speciﬁc for tubulointerstitial nephritis uveitis (TINU) syndrome?

explanation: The ﬁndings in tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis (TINU) are abnormal serum creatinine and decreased creatinine clearance, increased urinary beta-2 microglobulin, proteinuria, pyuria, hematuria, and urinary white cell casts. question: What type of macrophage produces the full spectrum of inﬂammatory and cytotoxic cytokines?
explanation: Resting macrophages are the classic scavenging cell, capable of phagocytosis and uptake of dead cell membranes, chemically modiﬁed extracellular protein (ie, acetylated or oxidized lipoproteins), sugar ligands, naked nucleic acids, and bacterial pathogens. Resting monocytes express at least 3 types of scavenging receptors but synthesize very low levels of proinﬂammatory cytokines. Scavenging can occur in the absence of inﬂammation. Primed macrophages are derived from resting macrophages that become primed by exposure to certain cytokines. Upon priming, these cells become positive for major histocompatibility (MHC) class II antigen and capable of functioning as antigen-presenting cells to T lymphocytes. Primed macrophages thus resemble dendritic cells. They can exit tissue sites by aﬀerent lymphatic vessels to reenter the lymph node. Activated macrophages are classically deﬁned as macrophages producing the full spectrum of inﬂammatory and cytotoxic cytokines; thus, they mediate and amplify acute inﬂammation, tumor killing, and major antibacterial activity. Epithelioid cells and giant cells represent diﬀerent terminal diﬀerentiations of the activated macrophage. question: A 45-year-old woman presents with sensitivity to light for 3 days. explanation: The correct answer is laboratory workup, chest X-ray, initiation of prednisolone drops every 2 hours and a cycloplegic agent. In a patient who presents with bilateral uveitis, a workup should always be done, and treatment should not be delayed. Initial treatment for anterior uveitis is a cycloplegic agent such as atropine or scopolamine, as well as prednisolone. Indications for workup of anterior uveitis include bilateral uveitis, more than 1 episode of uveitis, or ﬁrst episode of anterior uveitis with a positive review of systems. If a patient presents with unilateral uveitis for the ﬁrst time with a negative review of systems, a workup is not warranted. Medical history, review of systems, thorough ophthalmologic and general physical examination, and formulation of a working diﬀerential diagnosis are cornerstones of the workup of a patient with uveitis. They should precede any laboratory testing. Laboratory testing is not a substitute for a thorough, hands-on clinical evaluation. There is no one standardized battery of tests that ﬁts for all patients with uveitis. Rather, a tailored approach should be based on the most likely causes for each patient. After compiling a list of diﬀerential diagnoses based on the anatomical location and clinical characteristics of the inﬂammation, the ophthalmologist can order appropriate laboratory tests. Many patients require only a few diagnostic tests. Commonly ordered tests for anterior uveitis include: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) rapid plasma reagin (RPR) ﬂuorescent treponemal antibody-absorption (FTA-ABS) Lyme titer erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) antinuclear antibody (ANA) puriﬁed protein derivative (PPD) chest X-ray.

explanation: This is the patient's ﬁrst presentation at age 78 years, and given his lack of symptoms, the diagnosis is unlikely to be uveitic in nature. Although his age places him in the right demographic for lymphoma, his vitreous cavity is clear, making the diagnosis of primary intraocular lymphoma unlikely (although this should certainly be considered, as it is one of the masquerade syndromes for uveitis). explanation: First, one must realize that the patient has acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE), which is a white dot syndrome or inﬂammatory chorioretinopathy that is diagnosed by clinical presentation and ﬂuorescein angiography ﬁndings in the early phase of the disease. It presents like the case in the question stem, with sudden unilateral vision loss with central and paracentral scotomas, and involvement of the fellow eye within days to weeks. Photopsias may precede vision loss. As seen in the fundus photo, APMPPE is characterized by multiple scattered large (1-2 disc areas), ﬂat, yellow- white placoid lesions in the posterior pole, at the retinal pigment epithelium level, with minimal anterior segment inﬂammation and possible mild vitritis. Fluorescein angiography (FA) shows early hypoﬂuorescent lesions (either corresponding to or more numerous than the lesions seen on funduscopy), and late hyperﬂuorescent staining, as seen in the FA in the question. When neurologic symptoms are present in the setting of the above ﬁndings, then cerebral vasculitis must be ruled out with full neurologic evaluation, as it is a life- threatening entity associated with APMPPE. Out of the white dot syndromes, only APMPPE is associated with cerebral vasculitis. The other posterior uveitides associated with cerebral vasculitis are collagen vascular diseases such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Visual prognosis in APMPPE is favorable in that most patients regain 20/40 or better vision within 6 months. Residual visual dysfunction can occur in about 20% of patients. While systemic corticosteroids are not deﬁnitively beneﬁcial for visual outcomes, they are indicated for patients with CNS vasculitis. If this case presented with primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL) associated with primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL), then the retinal ﬁndings would classically include small multifocal subretinal granular inﬁltrates (Figure 4 Figure 4). Additionally, ﬂuorescein angiography would only show hypoﬂuorescent areas due to blockage from sub-RPE masses or RPE clumping. A leopard-spot pattern with alternating hyper- and hypoﬂuorescence may also be seen. Prognosis is poor for patients with PVRL and CNS involvement with 5-year overall survival of ~60% with treatment. explanation: Nontreponemal serum tests, such as serum VDRL and RPR, may be falsely elevated in several systemic conditions other than syphilis, including lupus erythematosus, leprosy, advanced age, intravenous drug abuse, bacterial endocarditis, tuberculosis (TB), vaccinations, infectious mononucleosis, HIV infection, pregnancy, atypical pneumonia, malaria, rickettsial infections, and other spirochetal infections. Additionally, nontreponemal serum tests may become negative in up to 30% of patients with late, untreated syphilis. As such, serum RPR alone is the least helpful in diagnosing a patient suspected of having syphilitic uveitis. Nontreponemal cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) tests are much more likely to remain positive in untreated disease, and the only nontreponemal test that should be performed on CSF samples is VDRL. Treponemal tests, such as FTA-ABS and MHA-TP, remain positive for the life of the patient infected with syphilis and are used to conﬁrm positive nontreponemal tests.

This is pathognomonic for sarcoidosis and the preferred treatment is immunosuppression with steroids or immunomodulatory medication. Systemic antibiotics would be indicated for adult inclusion cysts from trachoma. Systemic antihistamines are of beneﬁt for severe allergic conjunctivitis. Radiation may be beneﬁcial for localized conjunctival lymphoproliferative disorders.

question: What tissue is more eﬀectively evaluated with indocyanine green angiography than with ﬂuorescein angiography?
explanation: Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) is used to evaluate the choroid, including choroidal perfusion and lesions within the choroid. Imaging of the inner retina is best performed with optical coherence tomography. The pars plana is best imaged with wide-ﬁeld fundus photography and ﬂuorescein angiography. The ciliary body can be evaluated at least in part with gonioscopy, but anterior segment ultrasound biomicroscopy is excellent at imaging this structure.

question: Within what layer or layers of the healthy conjunctiva are mast cells typically found?
explanation: The conjunctival epithelium contains numerous goblet cells, Langerhans cells, and melanocytes. T lymphocytes are present in both the substantia propria and the epithelial layer. In healthy conjunctiva, mast cells are contained in the substantia propria. Once recruited by interleukin-5 and other mediators, mast cells migrate into the epithelium and are important in allergic immune reactions. The ﬁbrous layer contains vessels, nerves, and the glands of Krause.

question: What is the most common disorder associated with human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27 acute anterior uveitis?
explanation: Among patients with HLA-B27-associated anterior uveitis, ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the most common associated systemic manifestation (about 90% of patients with AS are HLA-B27+). Conversely, patients with AS are also the group most likely to develop acute anterior uveitis. However, most patients who test positive for the HLA-B27 antigen do not develop AS. Behçet disease is typically sporadic and not associated with HLA-B27. Systemic lupus erythematosus is an uncommon cause of anterior uveitis, and neither SLE nor toxoplasmosis is related to the HLA-B27 antigen. Host genetic factors may be related to the development of recurrent toxoplasmosis, but these factors are not yet well-deﬁned.

question: What cell type is primarily responsible for the nature of inﬂammation seen in ocular sarcoidosis?
explanation: Ocular sarcoidosis is characterized by a granulomatous inﬂammatory reaction due to a speciﬁc type of macrophage, the epithelioid cells. While monocytes are very similar to macrophages in function, monocytes are the circulating form of these cells, while macrophages are the tissue-bound form of these cells. Monocytes, therefore, are not responsible for the inﬂammatory reaction seen in ocular sarcoidosis. Neutrophils and eosinophils do not have a notable role in ocular sarcoidosis. immune recovery uveitis.

question: Cyclosporine has been proven eﬀective in controlled clinical studies for the treatment of what ocular inﬂammatory disease?

options.C: acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)

explanation: Cyclosporine is a calcineurin inhibitor that eliminates T-cell receptor signal transduction, down-regulates interleukin-2 (IL-2) gene transcription and receptor expression of CD4 T-lymphocytes. Cyclosporine has been shown to be eﬀective in treating Behçet disease-associated uveitis in a randomized, controlled clinical trial; it provided control of inﬂammation in 50% of patients. APMPPE usually does not require treatment; it is self-limited most of the time. Immune recovery uveitis is anterior or intermediate uveitis, which presents when immune status improves with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Usually, immune recovery uveitis is treated with local steroid therapy; systemic immunosuppressants are not indicated. An infectious etiology should be ruled out in postsurgical scleritis before systemic immunosuppressants are used. +.

question: When is a patient eligible to stop systemic anti-cytomegalovirus (anti-CMV) retinitis maintenance therapy?

options.A: once immune recovery-related cystoid macular edema (CME) is resolved
options.B: when CD4+ T lymphocytes are over 100 cells per microliter for 3-6 months
options.C: once intravitreal medications control the active infection
options.D: after 6 months of anti-CMV retinitis therapy

explanation: In patients with CMV retinitis who are on antiretroviral regimens and experience sustained immune recovery with CD4+ T lymphocytes over 100 cells per microliter for 3-6 months, systemic anti-CMV maintenance therapy may be safely discontinued. Antiretroviral therapy-naive patients may require only 6 months of anti-CMV therapy with good immune reconstitution, whereas antiretroviral therapy-experienced patients may require long-term maintenance therapy. Resolution of active infection or CME do not determine the timeline of systemic medication.

question: Why do autoimmune regulator (AIRE)–deﬁcient mice develop spontaneous uveitis?

options.A: Retinal antigens are overexpressed in regional lymph nodes.
options.B: Complement regulatory molecules are absent in the eyes of these animals.
options.C: The CD4:CD8 T helper cell ratio is reversed compared with that in wild type mice.

explanation: AIRE is a transcription factor used by the thymus in the process of establishing thymic tolerance. Early in life, the thymus expresses many cell-type–speciﬁc proteins; T-cell clones reactive to these proteins are deleted. This mechanism is important in the development of self- tolerance. Mice deﬁcient in AIRE do not express these proteins during development; thus, autoreactive T cells escape deletion, and the mice spontaneously develop a posterior uveitis.

question: Following resolution of the white dots, what ﬁnding suggests the diagnosis of multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS)?

options.C: punched-out lesions in the retinal periphery
options.D: granular pigment changes in the fovea

explanation: Subtle granular pigment changes in the fovea are present after the acute stage of MEWDS and they are considered pathognomonic for the disease. The ﬁnding can be very useful in diagnosing patients who present with symptoms after the white dots have faded. MEWDS patients do not typically develop peripheral punched-out lesions or peripapillary scarring, which can be present in ocular histoplasmosis syndrome and multifocal choroiditis. How do MHC class I molecules diﬀer structurally from MHC class II molecules?

options.A: Unlike MHC class II molecules, MHC class I molecules interact with CD4 T helper lymphocytes.
options.B: Unlike the beta chains in MHC class II molecules, the beta chain in MHC class I molecules is not polymorphic.
options.C: MHC class I molecules express receptors for the Fc portion of immunoglobulin E, whereas MHC class II molecules do not.
options.D: MHC class I molecules are composed of variable alpha and beta subunits, whereas class II molecules are composed of constant alpha and beta subunits.

explanation: Both MHC class I and II molecules are heterodimers, being made up of alpha and beta chains. For both MHC class I and II molecules, the alpha subunits are encoded by the MHC gene. Additionally, the beta subunits for MHC class II molecules are also encoded by the MHC gene. The beta subunit for MHC class I molecules (speciﬁcally the beta-2 microglobulin subunit) is encoded by the beta-2 microglobulin gene and is not polymorphic (is constant across all MHC class I molecules).

question: When testing a patient with a suspected sarcoidosis, what invasive evaluation has the lowest yield (sensitivity) of conﬁrming a diagnosis?
explanation: The most sensitive tests for detecting sarcoidosis are biopsy of a clinically apparent granuloma and computed tomography (CT) of the chest. However, biopsy of normal-appearing conjunctiva is very low yield. In patients with suggestive chest imaging, bronchoalveolar lavage, and biopsy can be diagnostic, with a sensitivity approaching 90% for ultrasound-guided biopsy of pulmonary granulomas. Gallium scans may increase the sensitivity over plain chest radiography, but interpretation usually requires other conﬁrmatory tests. valganciclovir.

explanation: Chronic postoperative endophthalmitis presents with recurrent bouts of indolent inﬂammation in an eye with previous history of ocular surgery, most commonly cataract surgery. Intravitreal corticosteroid injection should not be employed unless infectious endophthalmitis is ruled out. Chronic postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis is most commonly caused by Propionibacterium acnes (P acnes). Staphylococcus epidermis and Corynebacterium species can cause chronic postoperative endophthalmitis, too. P acnes may sequester itself between the intraocular lens (IOL) and the posterior capsule. This may present as whitish plaques. In such cases, intravitreal vancomycin is not curative; IOL explantation and complete capsulectomy, in addition to intravitreal vancomycin injection, should be performed. The specimens should be sent for stain, culture, and sensitivity.

question: One day ago, a patient developed a vesicular rash in the V dermatome. His primary care doctor started him on acyclovir and referred him for ophthalmologic examination. He does not have uveitis, and his ocular examination is unremarkable. What should the ophthalmologist do next?

options.A: Tell the primary care doctor and patient that there is no iritis, but uveitis may develop over weeks and follow-up will be arranged.
options.B: Tell the primary care doctor that there is no iritis and acyclovir will prevent the development of uveitis.
options.C: Tell the primary care doctor that there is no iritis and oral steroids should be used to prevent post- herpetic neuralgia.
options.D: Tell the primary care doctor and patient that there is no iritis and acyclovir may be stopped.

explanation: The vesicular rash in the V dermatome is typical for that of shingles or varicella-zoster virus (VZV). The anterior uveitis (iritis) associated with herpes zoster in the V dermatome can be mild or severe, but may develop weeks after the onset of disease. It can be associated with decreased corneal sensation, diﬀuse keratic precipitates (sometimes stellate), iris atrophy, and increased intraocular pressure (due to trabeculitis; these are common ﬁndings in viral anterior uveitis), but all these ﬁndings may or may not be found. It may be very long-lasting, and if mild and chronic, respond to very low doses of topical corticosteroids. Anterior uveitis secondary to VZV may occur without skin lesions (known as varicella-zoster sine herpete). Acyclovir may decrease the rate of anterior uveitis, though not in all cases, even at appropriate doses given in a timely manner. The use of oral steroids is ineﬀective in preventing post-herpetic neuralgia. 1 1.

question: What is the noninfectious systemic disease most commonly associated with scleritis?
explanation: About 40% of scleritis cases are associated with systemic disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and systemic lupus erythematosus are also associated with scleritis, but much less frequently. Multiple sclerosis is associated with intermediate uveitis and pars planitis, not scleritis.

question: A patient presents with 5 days of morning crusting, and yellow discharge. A clinical picture is shown here. Which cells are responsible for initiating the primary adaptive immunologic response in this patient?
explanation: This is a classic presentation for infectious--likely viral--conjunctivitis. The conjunctiva contains 2 types of antigen-presenting cells: Langerhans cells and macrophages. In the initial adaptive immune response, these antigen-presenting cells take up cellular debris and viral antigens. These antigens are processed and presented to T lymphocytes through the MHC class II molecule. These presenting cells activate and initiate responses from lymphocytes in the preauricular and submandibular lymph nodes to incite an immune response. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes are a subset of T lymphocytes that specialize in killing cells by either lysing infected cells or inducing apoptosis. A 54-year-old white woman presents with ﬂoaters, photopsia, and nyctalopia of several months' duration. On examination, visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes, and there are bilateral hypopigmented choroidal lesions and mild vitritis. What blood test is most consistent with the diagnosis?
explanation: HLA-A29 is associated with birdshot chorioretinopathy in more than 95% of cases, and has a sensitivity of 96% and speciﬁcity of 93%. Symptoms include ﬂoaters, photopsias, nyctalopia, and decreased contrast sensitivity. The clinical features are characterized by yellow choroidal lesions, vasculitis, and mild vitritis. When the clinical features are suggestive of birdshot, HLA-A29 testing is warranted and, if results are negative, should prompt consideration of another possible etiology or diagnosis. question: A patient with a long history of anterior uveitis wishes to have cataract surgery. What is a prerequisite for any elective intraocular surgery in uveitic eyes?

options.A: adequate view of the posterior segment

explanation: Any eye with chronic or recurrent uveitis may develop a cataract as a result of the inﬂammation or the corticosteroids used for treatment. Indications for cataract surgery in uveitic eyes are the same as for all cataracts: when the cataract causes functional impairment that interferes with activities of daily living; when the cataract is responsible for at least a portion of that visual decrease; and when functional improvement is likely to occur after cataract extraction. There is no prerequisite visual acuity. Additional considerations for cataract surgery in uveitic eyes are whether a cataract precludes the clinician from obtaining an adequate view of the fundus—thereby inhibiting appropriate monitoring of posterior segment disease or health. An adequate view of the posterior segment is therefore not a requirement. Uveitic eyes are at greater risk for postoperative complications than nonuveitic eyes. Thus, careful planning for surgery, including preoperative medical management and the timing of the procedure, is of utmost importance. The key to a successful visual outcome is meticulous long-term control of inﬂammation before proceeding with surgery. This may require immunomodulatory therapy in some patients, but is not a required treatment before cataract surgery. Common advice is to achieve the best control possible without ﬂare-ups for at least 3 months prior to cataract surgery.

question: What is a recommended therapy for Lyme disease?
explanation: Doxycycline, ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, and cefuroxime are recommended when antibiotic treatment of Lyme disease is necessary. There is currently no FDA-approved vaccine for Lyme disease in the United States. Atovaquone is an anti-parasitic drug that is not used for Lyme disease.

question: What congenital infection is most likely to manifest with intracranial calciﬁcations, chorioretinal scars, nystagmus, and optic atrophy?
explanation: Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is a single-stranded RNA virus of the Arenaviridae family; rodents are the natural hosts and reservoir. Transmission is thought to be airborne, from contamination of food by infected rodent excreta, or possibly from the bite of an infected animal. Symptomatic maternal illness occurs in approximately two-thirds of cases, with vertical transmission to the fetus occurring during episodes of maternal viremia. Systemic ﬁndings include macrocephaly, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calciﬁcations. Neurologic abnormalities, seizures, and mild cognitive impairment may be present. Ocular ﬁndings include macular and chorioretinal peripheral scarring, similar in morphology and distribution to that of congenital toxoplasmosis. Other ﬁndings include optic atrophy, strabismus, and nystagmus. Congenital rubella demonstrates cardiac malformations, chorioretinitis, cataracts, corneal clouding, microphthalmia, strabismus, glaucoma, and deafness. Cysticercosis may present with a leukocoric eye. When the brain is involved with cysticercosis, intracerebral calciﬁcations or hydrocephalus can be found. question: What feature is most consistent with uveitis in oligoarticular (also known as pauciarticular) juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA; formerly referred to as juvenile chronic arthritis and juvenile rheumatoid arthritis)?
explanation: Indolent, bilateral, chronic anterior uveitis, characterized by a low- grade anterior chamber cellular reaction, is the most common ocular manifestation of oligoarticular JIA. Other manifestations of JIA- associated, chronic anterior uveitis include ﬁne keratic precipitates, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient with acute unilateral anterior uveitis presents with an intraocular pressure of 35 mm Hg three days into treatment with frequent topical steroids. Examination with a slit lamp demonstrates a deep anterior chamber, 3+ cell and 2 clock hours of posterior synechiae. What is the most likely cause of increased intraocular pressure?
explanation: Elevated intraocular pressure in eyes with uveitis can result from several factors. In acute uveitis, intraocular pressure may be increased due to decreased aqueous outﬂow through inﬂamed trabecular meshwork, or through meshwork obstructed with inﬂammatory debris. Pupillary block glaucoma can result from circumferential posterior synechiae and seclusion of the pupil. Inﬂammation of the ciliary body can result in aqueous hyposecretion and result in hypotony or labile intraocular pressure when both the ciliary body and the trabecular meshwork are inﬂamed. Steroid-response glaucoma rarely occurs prior to 3 weeks of treatment, and clinicians should resist the urge to prematurely taper corticosteroids because of corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension.

question: A 72-year-old man reports several episodes of vision loss in his right eye over the past few months. He has no ocular history other than uncomplicated cataract surgery in both eyes 3 years ago. The patient has covered either eye and conﬁrms that the vision loss is isolated to his right eye. He describes the vision loss as a white out that comes on over several minutes, leaves him severely visually disabled for several hours, and then gradually clears back to his normal baseline vision over 1 to 2 hours. He has had eye examinations following each of these episodes in the past. They showed mild phacodonesis in the right eye but were otherwise unremarkable. Prior workup to rule out giant cell arteritis was negative. The patient is frustrated that despite multiple examinations, an etiology has not been found. What would be the most helpful thing to do on his visit today to help yield a diagnosis?

options.B: refer to cardiology for a Holter monitor

explanation: Whenever a patient complains of vision loss in 1 eye only, it is imperative to know whether the visual loss involves the right eye or the right ﬁeld of vision. Unless a patient has covered each eye alternately, they cannot know this. In this question, the patient was reliable and had conﬁrmed the vision loss was only in 1 eye. The second issue is the nature of the vision loss. Amaurosis fugax is characterized by temporary loss of all sight in the eye (a "blackout"). However, this patient describes a "white out," which is more characteristic of a transient obscuring of the ocular media, especially considering the long duration of the vision loss and the slow recovery over 1-2 hours. In any patient with symptoms suggestive of transient obscuring of the ocular media, who is also pseudophakic, uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome should be considered. In UGH syndrome, chaﬁng of the iris by the optic/bag complex or the haptics causes transient intraocular bleeds. Gonioscopy is the key to the diagnosis of UGH, especially after the vision has cleared. A small layer of hemorrhage in the inferior angle provides evidence of the transient bleed. Although originally described as a complication of iris chaﬁng by closed-loop anterior chamber intraocular lenses (IOLs), UGH syndrome is now more commonly seen with PCIOLs. Automated visual ﬁeld testing would be beneﬁcial if a homonymous defect were suspected, as opposed to loss of vision restricted to 1 eye. Likewise, referral to cardiology for a Holter monitor would be beneﬁcial if symptoms consistent with vertebro-basilar insuﬃciency were suspected; however, loss of vision restricted to 1 eye makes this less likely.
